cards.front: What is a “Company State”?
cards.back: A state set up by a company — in India, the East India Company's rule (1765–1858).

cards.front: Which Mughal emperor had two separate reigns, and why?
cards.back: Humayun — he ruled 1530–1540, was ousted by Sher Shah, then was restored 1555–1556.

cards.front: Where does the name “Mughal” come from, and what did the dynasty call itself?
cards.back: “Mughal” is a Persian corruption of “Mongol”; proud of their paternal ancestor Timur, they called themselves Timurids.

cards.front: From whom did Babur descend on his mother's and father's sides?
cards.back: Maternally from Genghis Khan; paternally from Timur (Tamerlane).

cards.front: What decided the First Battle of Panipat (1526)?
cards.back: Babur's small bronze cannons, which Ibrahim Lodi's larger army couldn't match — ending the Delhi Sultanate and founding the Mughal kingdom.

cards.front: Why were the three decisive battles (1526, 1556, 1761) all fought at Panipat?
cards.back: Geography: it sat on the Khyber invasion route, in the bottleneck between the Thar Desert and the Himalayas, with the Yamuna as a defensive choke-point.

cards.front: At which two battles did Sher Shah Suri defeat Humayun?
cards.back: Chausa (1539) and Kanauj (1540) — driving the Mughals out and founding the Suri dynasty (1540–55).

cards.front: What price did Humayun pay the Safavids of Iran to help retake his throne?
cards.back: He adopted Shia forms, ceded Kandahar to Iran, and promoted Persian culture at court.

cards.front: Who won the Second Battle of Panipat (1556) for the Mughals, and against whom?
cards.back: Bairam Khan, guardian of the young Akbar, defeated Hemu — securing Mughal rule for about 150 years.

cards.front: What was the Mansabdari system?
cards.back: The military-bureaucracy Akbar built to run the state, maintain its army, and keep royal control over a vast territory.

cards.front: How was a Mansabdar paid?
cards.back: In cash (a Naqdi Mansabdar) or by a Tankha Jagir — land whose revenue he kept, its holder called a Jagirdar.

cards.front: Into what categories was Mughal land divided?
cards.back: Jagir (revenue to Mansabdars), Khalisa (royal land, revenue to the King), and Inam (gifted land for a chosen beneficiary).

cards.front: Under Akbar's Zabti system, how was land revenue fixed and at what rate?
cards.back: By scientific survey of the land, set as a share of gross produce — about one-third under Akbar.

cards.front: How did a Zamindar differ from an Ijaradar for the peasant?
cards.back: Zamindar: bloodline-tied, commission capped by law (~10%, Nankar/Malikana). Ijaradar: bid for the collection right and kept all he extracted above the bid — capped only by what the peasant could endure.

cards.front: What is the difference between Khudkasht and Pahikasht peasants?
cards.back: Khudkasht cultivated the same land yearly, gaining occupancy rights (a Patta) but not ownership; Pahikasht were rootless share-croppers with no rights or protection.

cards.front: Who first imposed Jizya in India, and who institutionalised it?
cards.back: Muhammad bin Qasim first imposed it in Sindh (8th-century Arab conquest); Qutb-ud-din Aibak and his successors institutionalised it across the Delhi Sultanate (early 13th century).

cards.front: Which two Deccan kingdoms did Aurangzeb58-07 annex, and in what years?
cards.back: Bijapur (Adil Shahi Dynasty) in 1686 and Golconda (Qutb Shahi Dynasty) in 1687.

cards.front: Who first introduced Jizya in India, and who first institutionalised it?
cards.back: Muhammad bin Qasim introduced it in 712 CE; Qutb-ud-din Aibak06-10 first institutionalised it as Delhi Sultan.

cards.front: What was the sequence of Jizya abolition and re-introduction from Akbar56-05 to Farukhsiyar13-19?
cards.back: Akbar56-05 abolished it in 1564; Aurangzeb58-07 reintroduced in 1679; Zulfiqar Khan abolished in 1712; Farukhsiyar13-19 reintroduced in 1717.

cards.front: What happened to the Kashi Vishwanath temple in 1669, and who rebuilt it in 1780?
cards.back: Aurangzeb58-07 demolished it and replaced it with the Gyanvapi Mosque; Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore rebuilt it near the original site in 1780.

cards.front: Why did Aurangzeb58-07's executions of Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675) and Chhatrapati Sambhaji (1689) backfire?
cards.back: Both refused conversion and became martyrs, hardening anti-Mughal sentiment among Sikhs and Marathas rather than suppressing resistance.

cards.front: Why did the Mansabdari system become a source of instability after 1707?
cards.back: It ran on personal loyalty to the emperor, not the empire as an institution — weak Later Mughal emperors could not enforce loyalty, so Mansabdars pursued factionalism and carved out principalities instead.

cards.front: What three military innovations gave European forces an edge over the Mughals?
cards.back: File firing (rotating lines for continuous fire), grapeshot artillery (multiple bullets per shot), and the bayonet on the Brown Bess musket.

cards.front: What were the five main factions competing in the Mughal court after 1707, and which group did each key figure belong to?
cards.back: Irani (Shia Persian, e.g. Zulfiqar Khan); Turani (Sunni Turkish-Uzbek, e.g. Nizam-ul-Mulk24-48); Hindustani (e.g. Sayyid Brothers); Hindu (Rajputs/Jats, e.g. Sawai Jai Singh); Deccani (absorbed from Bijapur/Golconda).

cards.front: What was the Jagirdari crisis?
cards.back: A structural mismatch where demand for Jagirs far outstripped supply — caused by Aurangzeb58-07 absorbing Deccan nobles while declaring their lands Khalisa, then Later Mughals appointing more Mansabdars as Mughal-controlled territory shrank.

cards.front: What kingdom emerged from the 1695 peasant revolt, and who led it?
cards.back: The Jat Kingdom emerged from a peasant revolt under Churaman Jat, a Zamindar.

cards.front: How did the Sayyid Brothers bring down Farukhsiyar13-19 in 1719?
cards.back: They allied with Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath13-20 and 15,000 Maratha cavalry, killed Farukhsiyar13-19, and installed Md. Shah19-48 as their puppet emperor.

cards.front: Why did Nizam-ul-Mulk24-48 leave Delhi permanently in 1740?
cards.back: Having served as Wazir (1722–24) and recognised the imperial centre was beyond saving, he secured the Mansab of Governor of Hyderabad Suba in 1724 and departed for good in 1740.

cards.front: What did the Treaty of Bhopal (1738) concede to the Marathas?
cards.back: Legal Mughal recognition of Maratha control over all lands between the Chambal and Narmada rivers, and the Subah of Malwa.

cards.front: What decisive battle did Nadir Shah win against the Mughals, and what valuable assets did he take from Delhi?
cards.back: He won the Battle of Karnal (1739), then took the Peacock Throne and the Kohinoor diamond, extracting wealth estimated at ~100 crore rupees.

cards.front: How did Nadir Shah's 1739 invasion damage each of the five pillars of Mughal State power?
cards.back: Political: emperor publicly humiliated; Social: ~two lakh Delhi civilians massacred; Military: defeat invited the 1748 Afghan invasion; Economic: ~100 crore rupees extracted plus Peacock Throne/Kohinoor; Technological: resources for reform gone.

cards.front: What symbolic reversal occurred in 1752 and 1754 that marked the end of effective Mughal sovereignty?
cards.back: In 1752 the Mughal emperor accepted Maratha military protection; in 1754 the Marathas installed Alamgir II54-59 as their puppet emperor — the suppressed had become the kingmakers.

cards.front: What distinguishes a 'Successor State' from a 'Rebel State' in mid-18th century India?
cards.back: Successor States (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad) were carved out by powerful Mansabdars who extracted governing authority from the emperor; Rebel States (Marathas, Sikhs, Jats) openly rebelled against Mughal rule.

cards.front: In what years were the three Successor States formally established, and by whom?
cards.back: Bengal by Murshid Quli Khan in 1717, Awadh by Sadat Khan in 1722, Hyderabad by Nizam-ul-Mulk in 1724.

cards.front: What dual role did Nizam-ul-Mulk hold simultaneously between 1722 and 1724?
cards.back: He served as Wazir (PM/Imperial Diwan) at Delhi while simultaneously being Subahdar/Governor of Hyderabad.

cards.front: How did the Nizamat and Diwani branches of Bengal's administration differ in function and accountability?
cards.back: Nizamat (Nazim): law & order, criminal justice, defence — reported directly to Emperor; Diwani (Diwan): revenue, civil administration, civil justice — reported to Emperor via the Imperial Diwan (Wazir).

cards.front: What were the two anti-corruption functions of the Bakshi known as 'Dagh' and 'Chehra'?
cards.back: Dagh was branding of every Mansabdar's horse with an imperial mark for inspection; Chehra was recording every soldier's physical description (face, height, complexion) in a register.

cards.front: What was the significance of converting Tankha Jagirs into Vatan Jagirs in the Successor State formation?
cards.back: Vatan Jagirs were hereditary, so the emperor's historic tool of control — transferring jagirs at will — was surrendered, buying local Mansabdars' loyalty for the regional ruler.

cards.front: What was structurally unprecedented about Successor State rulers giving Mansabs to merchants and bankers?
cards.back: The Mansabdari system was traditionally lineage-based (military/noble bloodlines only); merging administrative rank with commercial wealth was a structural transformation of the system.

cards.front: How did Murshid Quli Khan end Akbar's checks and balances when he became Nazim of Bengal in 1717?
cards.back: He already held the Diwan post, so combining finance and executive authority in one man eliminated the separation Akbar had designed between the Nazim and Diwan.

cards.front: What role did the Jagat Seths play in the 1740 coup that brought Alivardi Khan to power in Bengal?
cards.back: The Jagat Seths backed Alivardi Khan's overthrow of Nawab Sarfaraz Khan; Alivardi then secured emperor Md Shah's formal approval by paying one crore rupees plus Sarfaraz's personal wealth.

cards.front: What was the outcome of the 1751 settlement between Alivardi Khan and Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur?
cards.back: Bhonsle received annual Chauth (one-fourth revenues) of Bengal and Bihar, plus direct control of Orissa — after which Alivardi stopped sending revenue to Delhi entirely.

cards.front: Why did Sadat Khan invite Nadir Shah to invade Delhi in 1739?
cards.back: He was angry that the Mir Bakshi Mansab had gone to Chin Qulich Khan (Nizam-ul-Mulk) instead of him, and sought Nadir Shah's backing to claim it.

cards.front: What event in 1753 marked Awadh's virtual break from the Mughal Empire?
cards.back: Safdar Jung was forced to resign as Wazir; after that, no more revenue was sent to Delhi and no imperial authority operated inside Awadh, though formal independence was never declared.

cards.front: What two military defeats forced Nizam-ul-Mulk to pay Chauth and Sardeshmukhi to the Marathas?
cards.back: He was defeated by the Marathas in 1728 and again in 1738, compelling him to pay Chauth (one-fourth) and Sardeshmukhi (10% hereditary Maratha claim in the Deccan).

cards.front: How did Hyderabad's Tankha-to-Vatan conversion and merchant Mansab appointments compare to the other two Successor States?
cards.back: Hyderabad saw the most pronounced transformation: Tankha-to-Vatan conversion was most aggressive and men of finance became Mansabdars on a larger scale than in Bengal or Awadh.

cards.front: What two steps did Nawab Saadatullah Khan take that moved the Carnatic towards de facto autonomy from Hyderabad?
cards.back: He moved the capital from Gingee to Arcot and made the Nawab post hereditary in his family without seeking Mughal or Nizam approval — adopting his nephew Dost Ali as heir.

cards.front: Which four Deccan Sultanates defeated the Vijayanagar Empire at the Battle of Talikota in 1565?
cards.back: Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, and Bidar formed the alliance that destroyed the Vijayanagar army, ending its effective power.

cards.front: What does the chapter identify as the gap that made the Indian subcontinent vulnerable to outside penetration by the EIC?
cards.back: Legitimacy and real power had come apart — the emperor retained formal authority and ceremonial usefulness while actual power rested with competing autonomous regional elites, each with its own fiscal and military interests.

cards.front: What were the terms Shivaji accepted under the Treaty of Purandhar (1665)?
cards.back: He surrendered 23 of his 35 forts, accepted Aurangzeb as Emperor, had son Sambhaji made a mansabdar of 5,000, and agreed to support Mughals against Bijapur.

cards.front: How did Shivaji kill Afzal Khan in 1659, and what weapons did he use?
cards.back: Shivaji killed the seven-feet-tall Afzal Khan during fake negotiations using his concealed Bagh Nakh (Tiger Claws) and a Bichhwa (dagger).

cards.front: Where and when was Shivaji coronated, and what did he name his kingdom?
cards.back: Shivaji was coronated at Raigarh in 1674 as Chhatrapati; his kingdom, covering the Marathi-speaking region, was called Svarajya ('own rule').

cards.front: How did a Saranjam differ from a Vatan/Watan in the Maratha land-grant system?
cards.back: Saranjam: a Tankha Jagir for military commanders — temporary, tied to service, NOT heritable. Vatan: a hereditary right for civil officials like Patils and Deshmukhs — passed within the family.

cards.front: What was the Jaladurg doctrine, and which forts exemplified it?
cards.back: Sea forts built on rocky islands or peninsulas along the coastline to shelter docked vessels and keep enemy ships at distance with coastal cannons; examples: Sindhudurg, Vijaydurg, Suvarnadurg.

cards.front: Why is Shivaji called the Father of the Modern Indian Navy?
cards.back: He relied entirely on indigenous human resources, engineering, and strategy — never on European naval architects — recruiting from local Koli and Bhandari coastal communities.

cards.front: How did the three main Maratha warship types — Ghurabs, Galbats, and Shibars — differ in function?
cards.back: Ghurabs: gunboats with heavy artillery. Galbats: fast, manoeuvrable rowboats that towed Ghurabs and chased enemies. Shibars and Pals: larger vessels for transport and heavier engagements.

cards.front: What are the eight ministers of the Maratha Ashtapradhan and their portfolios?
cards.back: Peshwa (PM), Amatya (Finance), Sachiv (Correspondence), Sumanta (Foreign Affairs), Senapati (Military), Panditrao (Religious Affairs), Nyayadhish (Justice), Waqenavis (Intelligence).

cards.front: How did the judicial authority differ between Svarajya and Samrajya?
cards.back: In Svarajya, the final judicial decision rested with the Peshwa. In Samrajya, it rested with the respective Maratha Sardar.

cards.front: What did the Treaty of Warna (1731) settle, and what two Chhatrapati lines did it create?
cards.back: It ended the Shahu–Tarabai civil war by giving Kolhapur to Sambhaji II; thereafter Shahu's line ruled from Satara and Sambhaji II's line ruled from Kolhapur.

cards.front: How did Chauth and Sardeshmukhi differ in who paid them and what scope they covered?
cards.back: Chauth (25% of revenue) was collected only from states outside the Maratha Empire. Sardeshmukhi (10% of land revenue) could be collected both internally and externally.

cards.front: How was Chauth split when a Maratha Sardar (not the Peshwa/Chhatrapati) collected it from an outside state?
cards.back: Mokasa 66% kept by the Sardar; Babti 25% sent to the Chhatrapati; Sahotra 6% to the Pant Sachiv; Nadgaunda 3% at the Chhatrapati's discretion.

cards.front: What did the Treaty of Sangola (February 1750) transfer, and who signed it?
cards.back: Chhatrapati Ramraja signed it under Peshwa Nana Saheb40-61's pressure, transferring all real political power from the Chhatrapati to the Peshwa.

cards.front: What three concessions did the Marathas gain from the Mughals through the Sayyid Brothers deal of 1719?
cards.back: Formal Mughal recognition of Maratha autonomy in Maharashtra; Chauth of Malwa and Gujarat; right to collect Chauth and Sardeshmukhi from the six Deccan Mughal provinces.

cards.front: What did the Treaty of Bhopal (1738) award the Marathas, and what had they already held since 1729?
cards.back: The Suba of Malwa and sovereignty over all lands between the Chambal and Narmada rivers — formalising what the Marathas had controlled de facto since 1729.

cards.front: Who comprised Abdali's alliance at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761), and what were the troop strengths on each side?
cards.back: Abdali's side (~60,000): Abdali himself, Rohillas under Najib-ud-Daula, Bangash Pathans under Ahmad Khan, and Awadh under Shuja-ud-Daula; versus Marathas (~50,000).

cards.front: What was the decisive strategic consequence of the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) for India's political future?
cards.back: It created a power vacuum at the centre — deciding neither Marathas nor Abdali would rule India — which the British EIC eventually filled by defeating regional states one by one.

cards.front: Why have so many empire-deciding battles been fought near Panipat?
cards.back: Panipat lies on the gateway to Delhi for armies advancing from Central Asia through the Khyber Pass; its open plains suited large armies, weather aided long campaigns, and proximity to Delhi eased supply.

cards.front: Which three Rebel States emerged alongside the Marathas as the Mughal Empire weakened in the 18th century?
cards.back: The Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur (East Rajasthan), and the two Afghan kingdoms of Farrukhabad (est. 1714) and Rohilkhand (crystallised 1737–40).

cards.front: Who led the first organised Jat revolt, and in what year did it occur?
cards.back: Zamindar Gokla led the first organised Jat revolt in 1669, triggered by harsh Mughal land revenue policies.

cards.front: Who formally established the Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur, and what were his tenure years?
cards.back: Churaman Jat (1695–1721) formally established the Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur in East Rajasthan.

cards.front: What three administrative reforms did Maharaja Surajmal introduce during the Jat Kingdom's peak (1756–63)?
cards.back: He recruited European soldiers to modernise the military, introduced a Mughal-style revenue system, and removed relatives from court positions to reduce factionalism.

cards.front: What was the maximum territorial extent of the Jat State at its peak under Surajmal?
cards.back: Delhi to Agra and from the Chambal River to the Ganga, covering parts of present-day Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, and Rajasthan.

cards.front: Why did the Jat–Maratha alliance fail before the 3rd Battle of Panipat (1761)?
cards.back: Surajmal wanted to deploy guerrilla warfare while Maratha commander Sadasiv Rao Bau insisted on traditional warfare; they could not agree on strategy.

cards.front: How did Sher Shah Suri defeat Humayun, and what did this inaugurate?
cards.back: Sher Shah Suri defeated Humayun at the Battle of Kanauj in 1540, driving him into exile in Persia and beginning the Suri Interregnum (1540–55).

cards.front: What four administrative and infrastructural reforms is Sher Shah Suri credited with?
cards.back: He created a Suba–Sarkar–Pargana administrative hierarchy, upgraded the Grand Trunk Road, set up the Dak Chowki postal relay, and introduced the standardised silver Rupiya coin.

cards.front: How did Sher Shah Suri change land revenue collection compared to earlier practice?
cards.back: He commissioned careful land surveys and fixed the revenue demand directly with the peasant, cutting out the middleman Zamindar.

cards.front: How did Md Khan Bangash obtain the basis for founding Farrukhabad, and in what year was the city established?
cards.back: He provided 12,000 troops to Farukhsiyar (1713–19) and was rewarded with the rank of Nawab and revenue assignments; he founded the city of Farrukhabad in 1714.

cards.front: What role did Safdar Jung play in Farrukhabad's history in 1749?
cards.back: Safdar Jung (Nawab of Awadh and Mughal Wazir) engineered Qaim Khan's death in battle and formally annexed Farrukhabad to Awadh, then plundered it.

cards.front: What happened to Farrukhabad at the 3rd Battle of Panipat (1761) and immediately after?
cards.back: Ahmad Khan fought alongside Ahmad Shah Abdali; after the Maratha defeat he recovered his full dominions including the half ceded to Holkar and Scindia in 1752.

cards.front: What does the term 'Rohilla' mean, and where does it come from?
cards.back: Rohilla derives from 'Roh,' the Afghan homeland; Rohilkhand therefore means 'the land of the Rohillas' — settled Afghan mercenaries who consolidated power in Katehr.

cards.front: What event in 1739 converted Ali Md Khan from a mercenary strongman into an independent ruler of Rohilkhand?
cards.back: Nadir Shah's devastating invasion of Delhi paralysed the Mughal State; Ali Md Khan stopped paying taxes and began ruling Katehr as an independent power.

cards.front: How did the Mughal Emperor formally recognise Rohilkhand's autonomy, and when?
cards.back: In 1740, Emperor Md Shah (1719–48) granted Ali Md Khan the title of Subadar; Katehr was officially renamed Rohilkhand and functioned as an autonomous state under nominal Mughal sovereignty.

cards.front: How did Rohilkhand end — what force annexed it, and under what treaty authority?
cards.back: Awadh, with EIC help under the military alliance from the Treaty of Allahabad (1765), annexed most of Rohilkhand in 1774; a small remnant became the autonomous state of Rampur under Bareilly.

cards.front: How did the three Rebel States — Jats, Farrukhabad, and Rohilkhand — differ in the way they built their kingdoms?
cards.back: Jats: Zamindar-led agrarian revolt rising upward to territory. Farrukhabad: Mughal court politics downward — troops for an emperor → Nawab title → city. Rohilkhand: two-decade ground-level mercenary consolidation, then outright defiance in the 1739 Delhi crisis.

cards.front: What single structural weakness did all three Rebel States — Jats, Farrukhabad, and Rohilkhand — share that explains their collapse?
cards.back: Each depended on external support to reach its peak — Abdali for the Afghan kingdoms, Maratha tactical backing for the Jats — and collapsed once that external prop was removed.

cards.front: Who founded Sikhism, when did he live, and where did he finally settle?
cards.back: Guru Nanak Dev (1469–1539) settled at Kartarpur, present-day Pakistan, after 30 years of spiritual journeys covering ~30,000 km.

cards.front: What was the institution of Langar established by Guru Nanak Dev?
cards.back: A free communal kitchen set up at Kartarpur to promote equality by providing meals to all, regardless of caste or status.

cards.front: Which two executions turned the Sikh community from a peaceful movement toward a martial one, and who ordered each?
cards.back: Guru Arjan Dev (5th Guru) executed by Jahangir in 1606, and Guru Teg Bahadur (9th Guru) executed by Aurangzeb in Delhi in 1675.

cards.front: What was the Khalsa, and when and where was it established?
cards.back: A Sikh military organisation created by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699 at Anandpur to defend the Sikh Panth and struggle for a Sikh State.

cards.front: Why did Guru Gobind Singh declare the Guru Granth Sahib Ji as the final Guru rather than appointing a human successor?
cards.back: To prevent community tension between the Jat-dominated Khalsa and the Khatri community (to which all ten Gurus belonged) by vesting authority in the holy book permanently.

cards.front: What was the Battle of Chappar Chiri (1710), and what did it lead to?
cards.back: Banda Bahadur defeated and killed Wazir Khan there, which led to the conquest of Sirhind and the establishment of a Sikh State between the rivers Ravi and Jamuna.

cards.front: What three reasons caused the collapse of Banda Bahadur's Sikh State by 1715?
cards.back: Khatri traders turned against him (trade disrupted); Mughals used divide-and-rule via Ijaradari offers to co-opt Khatris; Hindu Jat zamindars like Churaman Jat switched sides for dynastic recognition.

cards.front: What were Misls, and how did they govern Punjab after Banda Bahadur's defeat?
cards.back: Kinship-based clans that united against Afghan invasions but otherwise operated independently; conquered lands were distributed among members in proportion to military and monetary contribution.

cards.front: What event gave Ranjit Singh the platform to establish dominance over the Misl chiefs, and in what year was he coronated King?
cards.back: His crucial role in defeating Zaman Shah's third Afghan invasion of 1799 gave him the platform; he was coronated King of the Sikh State in 1801.

cards.front: What were the key terms of the 1809 Treaty of Amritsar between Ranjit Singh and the EIC?
cards.back: EIC recognised Ranjit Singh as sovereign of Punjab; the Sutlej River was fixed as the border; Ranjit Singh was free to expand north and west without British interference.

cards.front: Who conquered Peshawar for Ranjit Singh in 1834, and what was his reputation among the Afghans?
cards.back: Hari Singh Nalwa conquered Peshawar; his reputation was so fearsome that Afghan mothers used his name to frighten unruly children.

cards.front: What was the 1838 Tripartite Treaty, and who were its three parties?
cards.back: A treaty between the Sikh State, the EIC, and Shah Shuja of Afghanistan aimed at establishing British indirect rule in Afghanistan as a buffer against a feared Russian invasion of British India.

cards.front: How did the Jagirdari and direct-revenue land systems coexist under Ranjit Singh's revenue policy?
cards.back: Only 40% of land was under Jagirdari; revenue from the remaining 60% went directly to the King, giving him considerable monetary power independent of jagirdars.

cards.front: What was a Kardar in Ranjit Singh's administration?
cards.back: The chief administrative officer at the Taluqa (district) level, combining the roles of revenue collector, local magistrate, police chief, and customs officer.

cards.front: How did Ranjit Singh's key ministerial appointments reflect the secular nature of his State?
cards.back: Fakir Azizuddin (Muslim) served as Foreign Minister; Dewan Dina Nath (Hindu) served as Finance Minister — key posts held across religious lines.

cards.front: What was a Vatan Jagir in Akbar's arrangement with Rajput chiefs?
cards.back: A Rajput chief's home territory recognised within the Mughal framework — land remained theirs, but they accepted the Emperor as sovereign and paid tribute.

cards.front: What triggered the Rajput revolt against Aurangzeb in 1680?
cards.back: Aurangzeb's interference in Marwar's succession after a child came to the throne, combined with Mewar's aggressive expansion, drove both kingdoms to revolt.

cards.front: Why did the 1680 Rajput revolt against Aurangzeb collapse?
cards.back: Other Rajput chiefs refused to join, fearing that a successful revolt would let Mewar dominate all of Rajputana — so each stood aside.

cards.front: What happened to Rajput states after the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05)?
cards.back: The EIC replaced the Marathas as the regional power and signed Subsidiary Alliances with the Rajput states.

cards.front: What five Jantar Mantars did Sawai Jai Singh build, and which is the largest?
cards.back: Delhi (1724), Jaipur (1734), Ujjain, Mathura, and Varanasi; Jaipur's is the largest and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2010).

cards.front: What astronomical work did Sawai Jai Singh produce from his Jantar Mantar observations?
cards.back: Zij-i-Muhammad Shahi (1733), dedicated to Muhammad Shah, correcting accumulated errors in older Islamic and Hindu astronomical tables.

cards.front: Why is Jaipur called the first planned city of modern India?
cards.back: It was designed by Vidyadhar Bhattacharya on Vastu Shastra principles with a grid-pattern layout, founded in 1727 by Sawai Jai Singh.

cards.front: What was the significance of the Battle of Colachel (1741)?
cards.back: Marthanda Varma's army defeated the Dutch East India Company, permanently ending Dutch political and military ambitions in Kerala.

cards.front: What was the Kundara Proclamation (1809) and who issued it?
cards.back: A public call by Velu Thampi Dalawa, Prime Minister of Travancore, urging the people to rise against British control after the humiliating Subsidiary Alliance of 1805.

cards.front: How did Haider Ali seize power in Mysore in 1761?
cards.back: He overthrew NanjRaj, the corrupt and powerful Prime Minister who had reduced the Wodeyars to figureheads, while keeping the Wodeyar as nominal head of State.

cards.front: What were Risalas in Haider Ali's reformed army?
cards.back: European-model regiments, each with a commander directly appointed by the King, its own weapons, transport, and supplies, capable of independent action.

cards.front: What is Military Fiscalism as practised in Mysore?
cards.back: The systematic generation of State wealth — through expanded Khalisa land, direct tax collection, irrigation, cash crops, and sericulture — as a deliberate foundation for military power.

cards.front: How did Khalisa land differ from Jagirdari land in Mysore's revenue system?
cards.back: Khalisa: revenue went directly to the State treasury. Jagirdari: revenue was assigned to nobles or commanders. Mysore expanded Khalisa and minimised Jagirdari to maximise State income.

cards.front: What military innovation did Haider Ali and Tipu Sultan develop, and who later copied it?
cards.back: Iron-cased rocket artillery with a 2 km range — fully indigenous; William Congreve's British rockets of the early 19th century drew directly from Tipu's designs.

cards.front: How did Tipu Sultan formally assert independence in 1785?
cards.back: He declared independence from both the Wodeyars and the Mughal Emperor, and requested a sanad from the Khalifa recognising him as an independent ruler.

cards.front: What symbolic acts connected Tipu Sultan to the French Revolution?
cards.back: He planted a Tree of Liberty in Mysore and became a member of the Jacobin Club, the radical organisation at the heart of the French Revolution.

cards.front: When and how did Tipu Sultan's rule end?
cards.back: He died at Seringapatam during the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War in 1799, breaking Mysore's power after four wars spanning 1767–1799.

cards.front: What profit did Vasco Da Gama's first cargo earn when sold in Europe after his 1498 voyage?
cards.back: 800% profit — so lucrative that by the 1600s one kilogram of clove in Europe cost the equivalent of one kilogram of gold.

cards.front: Which three regions and their primary commodities drove the early Asia–Europe trade?
cards.back: Indonesia (spices), India (textiles + Malabar spices), and China (silk and tea).

cards.front: What event in 1453 forced European powers to seek a new sea route to Asia?
cards.back: The Ottoman Empire captured Constantinople and blockaded the traditional land trade routes connecting Europe to Asia.

cards.front: What did the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) establish, and who mediated it?
cards.back: Pope Alexander VI drew an imaginary line ~1,185 miles west of Cape Verde Islands — lands east went to Portugal, lands west to Spain.

cards.front: What was the first permanent Portuguese factory in India, and who established it?
cards.back: Cochin (1500), established by Pedro Cabral after his Calicut factory was destroyed by Arab merchants.

cards.front: What was the Portuguese Cartaz System?
cards.back: A naval licensing system under which all non-Portuguese ships had to buy a pass (Cartaz) and pay a fee to sail safely in the Indian Ocean — pay or face attack.

cards.front: What was the Blue Water Policy introduced by Almeida (1505–09)?
cards.back: Emphasis on naval supremacy over territorial conquest — dominating oceans and trade routes rather than building a large land empire, since India had powerful land-based States.

cards.front: What was the significance of the Battle of Diu (1509)?
cards.back: Almeida defeated a joint Muslim naval coalition of Gujarat, Mamluk Egypt, Zamorin of Calicut (backed by Ottoman Empire and Venice), consolidating Portuguese naval supremacy for the next century.

cards.front: How did Almeida's Blue Water Policy differ from Albuquerque's approach to Portuguese India?
cards.back: Almeida: naval supremacy only, no land conquest. Albuquerque: territorial expansion — annexed Goa (1510), introduced Luso-Indian intermarriage policy, and built a colonial State.

cards.front: Which crops did the Portuguese introduce to India from the Americas?
cards.back: Tobacco, red chillies, papaya, pineapple, and guava — brought via the Columbian Exchange (cocoa and rubber came only in the British period).

cards.front: Where was the first Dutch factory in India, and when was it established?
cards.back: Masulipatnam in the Northern Sarkars (Andhra Pradesh), in 1605 — on a farman from the Sultan of Golconda.

cards.front: What were the three Dutch HQ locations in India and their respective roles?
cards.back: Pulicat (Fort Geldria, main HQ 1610–1690); Nagapattinam (main HQ 1690–1795); Cochin = HQ of Dutch Malabar only (NOT overall HQ); Chinsura = HQ of Dutch Bengal only.

cards.front: What did the Royal Charter of 1600 grant to the English East India Company?
cards.back: A 15-year monopoly over England's trade with the East Indies, the right to carry gold out of England, and management by a Governor, Deputy Governor, and 24 members.

cards.front: What was the most significant legal change in Cromwell's EIC Charter of 1657?
cards.back: It reorganised the EIC into a permanent joint-stock company — capital stayed invested continuously rather than being raised and dissolved voyage by voyage.

cards.front: What quasi-State powers did the EIC's Charter of 1661 confer?
cards.back: Right to build forts, command troops, make war and peace, and exercise civil and criminal jurisdiction over their Indian settlements.

cards.front: What was the distinction between the 1612 Battle of Swally and the 1613 Farman in establishing the EIC at Surat?
cards.back: 1612 = Captain Thomas Best's military victory over the Portuguese and a local Mughal governor's temporary permission; 1613 = Jahangir's imperial farman making the Surat factory legally permanent.

cards.front: What did Thomas Roe secure from Jahangir's court (1615–19) for the EIC?
cards.back: A Royal Farman (1618) granting the EIC the right to establish factories throughout the Mughal Empire and liberal trading rights including lower customs duties.

cards.front: How did the Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 1661 transfer Bombay to the English EIC?
cards.back: Portugal gave Bombay (and Tangier) as dowry when Princess Catherine of Braganza married King Charles II; the Crown then leased Bombay to the EIC in 1668 at £10 per annum.

cards.front: What powers did the 1661 Charter grant the EIC in India?
cards.back: Right to build forts, command troops, make war and peace, and exercise civil and criminal jurisdiction over its settlements.

cards.front: By 1857, how much of India's territory and population did the EIC control?
cards.back: 63% of India's territory and 78% of its population.

cards.front: Why is the Anglo-Mughal War of 1686–90 also called Child's War?
cards.back: Named after Josiah Child (Chairman of EIC's Court of Directors in London) and John Child (Governor of Bombay and General of all EIC forces in India).

cards.front: What did the 1691 Farman grant the EIC, and at what annual cost?
cards.back: Restored EIC's old privileges and gave it the right to duty-free trade in Bengal in exchange for Rs 3,000 per annum.

cards.front: Why did Aurangzeb pardon the EIC after defeating it militarily in 1690 rather than expelling the British?
cards.back: EIC trade brought forex and gold into India, Indian bankers and merchants depended on it, and it was economically useful even amid Aurangzeb's own wars.

cards.front: Which European war triggered each of the three Carnatic Wars?
cards.back: 1st (1746–48): Austrian War of Succession (1740–48); 2nd (1749–54): succession disputes in Carnatic and Hyderabad; 3rd (1756–63): Seven Years' Global War (1756–63).

cards.front: What happened at the Battle of Adyar/St Thome (1746) and why did it matter?
cards.back: Roughly 1,000 French-trained troops destroyed the Nawab of Carnatic's 10,000-strong cavalry, proving European military methods superior to traditional Indian armies.

cards.front: What three military advantages gave Europeans decisive superiority over Indian armies in the Carnatic Wars?
cards.back: Superior mobile artillery, disciplined infantry formations (including infantry squares), and regular cash salaries that kept sepoys professional and loyal.

cards.front: What did the Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748) decide about Madras?
cards.back: Both Britain and France agreed to return each other's possessions; Madras was handed back to the EIC, reversing Dupleix's military gains in India.

cards.front: In the 2nd Carnatic War, whom did France back versus the EIC — in both Hyderabad and Carnatic?
cards.back: France: Muzaffar Jung (Hyderabad) and Chanda Sahib (Carnatic); EIC: Nasir Jung (Hyderabad) and Md Ali (Carnatic).

cards.front: How did Robert Clive turn the tide for the EIC during the 2nd Carnatic War?
cards.back: With roughly 500 men (200 Europeans, 300 sepoys) he captured the unguarded capital Arcot and held it through a 53-day counter-siege, breaking French momentum.

cards.front: What were the key terms of the Treaty of Pondicherry (1754) that ended the 2nd Carnatic War?
cards.back: French influence remained in Hyderabad via Bussy; French factories in Pondicherry and Carnatic retained; Md Ali became Nawab of Carnatic, giving EIC influence there.

cards.front: What was Dupleix's 'blueprint for empire' — the strategic method he pioneered in the 2nd Carnatic War?
cards.back: Backing chosen candidates in local succession disputes to install friendly rulers, then extracting territory, revenue, and influence as payment for military support.

cards.front: Which battle was most decisive in the 3rd Carnatic War, and in what year?
cards.back: Battle of Wandiwash (1760), after which the French lost everywhere including Pondicherry, their headquarters since 1701.

cards.front: How did the French EIC and British EIC differ structurally, and why did it matter in the Carnatic Wars?
cards.back: French EIC was a State PSU with weak finances and unpaid troops; British EIC was a private joint-stock firm with deep capital and wealth accumulated after Plassey 1757.

cards.front: What did the Treaty of Paris (1763) leave France with in India?
cards.back: Only five small trading posts — Pondicherry, Mahe, Karaikal, Yanam, and Chandernagore — barred from maintaining a strong army or fortifying its bases.

cards.front: What did the Treaty of Hyderabad (1766) settle, and what did Hyderabad receive in return?
cards.back: Hyderabad formally ceded the Northern Sarkars to the EIC in exchange for Rs 7 lakh annually and protection against the Marathas and Mysore.

cards.front: Which Indian state was first to sign a Subsidiary Alliance with the EIC, and in which year?
cards.back: Hyderabad, in 1798; Mysore followed in 1799, Travancore in 1805, and Carnatic was annexed in 1801.

cards.front: Why was the 1717 Imperial Farman called the 'Magna Carta of the Company'?
cards.back: Issued by Farrukhsiyar, it gave EIC duty-free trade across Bengal, Deccan and Gujarat, the right to use the Royal Mint, and permission to rent 38 villages near Calcutta.

cards.front: What did EIC receive in exchange for the 1691 Farman granting duty-free trade in Bengal?
cards.back: EIC paid 3,000 rupees per annum to the Bengal Suba — accepted because EIC trade was economically beneficial and brought foreign exchange into India.

cards.front: What were Dastaks, and how were they misused by EIC officials?
cards.back: Dastaks were EIC-issued permits certifying goods as company-owned and thus exempt from export duty; officials used them for private trade and sold them to other exporters, costing Bengal custom revenue.

cards.front: How did Interlopers differ from Free Merchants in EIC-era India?
cards.back: Interlopers: non-EIC British traders who exported independently, violating the Royal Charter back in Britain. Free Merchants: non-EIC traders who sold goods to EIC in India only, making their trade technically legal under British law.

cards.front: Why did Nawab Alivardi Khan tolerate EIC's fortification of Calcutta while his successor Siraj-ud-daula did not?
cards.back: Alivardi Khan chose diplomacy because EIC trade benefited Bengal economically; Siraj was young, assertive, and had stopped Dastak misuse — directly threatening EIC officials' private fortunes.

cards.front: What was the Black Hole Tragedy, and how did later historians revise the colonial account?
cards.back: British prisoners were locked overnight in a small Fort William guardroom; J.Z. Holwell claimed 146 imprisoned and 123 dead, but modern historians put the actual death toll at approximately 30–40.

cards.front: What role did Mir Jafar play at the Battle of Plassey (1757)?
cards.back: Mir Jafar, effectively the Bengal army's commander, conspired with Clive to keep the bulk of the Bengal army from fighting, ensuring Siraj-ud-daula's easy defeat.

cards.front: What did Robert Clive personally receive from the financial settlement after Plassey?
cards.back: Clive received 2,34,000 pounds outright plus a personal jagir worth 35,000 pounds per annum.

cards.front: How did the Battle of Plassey change the direction of gold flows between Britain and India?
cards.back: Before Plassey, gold was shipped from Britain to buy Indian goods; after Plassey, Bengal's own Diwani revenues funded Indian and Chinese purchases, and gold flowed out of India to Britain — beginning the Drain of Wealth.

cards.front: Who were Gomastas, and why did they harm Indian merchants after Plassey?
cards.back: Gomastas were Indian agents employed by EIC officials to procure goods directly from peasants and artisans, cutting out Indian merchants and paying no domestic taxes — giving EIC an unfair competitive advantage.

cards.front: What two reforms did Mir Qasim introduce that provoked EIC into war?
cards.back: He punished zamindars who underreported land revenue, and abolished all internal duties on domestic trade to level the playing field between Indian merchants and EIC officials doing untaxed trade.

cards.front: Who were the three allied commanders against EIC at the Battle of Buxar (1764)?
cards.back: Mir Qasim (former Nawab of Bengal), Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh, and Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II.

cards.front: What was the Dual Government of Bengal (1765–72), and who held what power under it?
cards.back: EIC held the Diwani (revenue, civil administration) while the Nawab retained the Nizamat (law, order, criminal justice) in name; in practice EIC appointed the Deputy Nawab and ran both wings.

cards.front: What legal fiction did the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) use to legitimise EIC's rule in Bengal?
cards.back: EIC absorbed itself into Mughal legal structure as a Mansabdar — paying Shah Alam II an annual tribute of 26 lakh rupees — making Bengal EIC's Watan Jagir in formal Mughal terms.

cards.front: Why did EIC end the Dual Government and establish Direct Rule over Bengal in 1772?
cards.back: The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 killed an estimated one-third of Bengal's population; revenue collection and law and order collapsed because neither EIC nor Nawab accepted responsibility for relief.

cards.front: What were the three elements of Indirect Rule that the Treaty of Allahabad formally installed in Bengal?
cards.back: A puppet Nawab, a British Resident stationed at court, and the Resident's control over the puppet — with EIC also holding the legal right to appoint and remove the Deputy Nawab.

cards.front: What was the Policy of Ring Fence, and how was it applied to Awadh in 1765?
cards.back: Ring Fence meant creating a military buffer around EIC's core territory by allying with neighbouring states; Awadh was treaty-bound to assist if Bengal was attacked, and an EIC army was permanently stationed there at Awadh's expense.

cards.front: What distinguishes the Battle of Plassey (1757) from the Battle of Buxar (1764) in terms of military character and consequence?
cards.back: Plassey was a conspiracy not a battle — Mir Jafar held Bengal's army back; Buxar was a real, closely fought engagement. Plassey gave EIC political supremacy; Buxar gave EIC the legal right to rule through the Diwani.

cards.front: What was Fort William College (1800) established for?
cards.back: To train British civil servants in Indian languages, laws, and customs before posting them to the districts.

cards.front: What was the legal difference between the Company's Army and the King's Army operating in India?
cards.back: The Company's Army was the EIC's own private military; the King's Army was the British State's regiments — legally distinct, with the EIC reimbursing the Crown for Royal troops deployed.

cards.front: What did Pitt's India Act 1784 prohibit regarding war, and on what single ground could the Governor-General still act?
cards.back: It banned offensive war without prior authorisation from the Court of Directors or Board of Control; the GG could act unilaterally only on grounds of defence.

cards.front: How did Wellesley justify re-initiating conquest despite Pitt's India Act 1784 banning offensive war?
cards.back: He overhyped the threat of a Napoleon–Tipu Sultan alliance, citing Napoleon's 1798 Egyptian campaign and Tipu's communications with the French.

cards.front: Who pioneered the first proto-form of the Subsidiary Alliance, where, and how was it funded?
cards.back: Dupleix (French EIC Governor General) installed it at Hyderabad in 1751 — a French force under Bussy was stationed there, paid out of the revenues of the Northern Sarkars.

cards.front: How did the Treaty of Allahabad 1765 (Awadh) differ from Wellesley's full Subsidiary Alliance?
cards.back: ToA 1765 was a mini-SA: an EIC army in Awadh paid by subsidy and a British Resident stationed, but Awadh's own army was NOT disbanded and Foreign Policy was NOT taken over — the full SA came only in 1801.

cards.front: What was the legal reason the Subsidiary Alliance specifically required the Indian State to surrender Foreign Policy?
cards.back: The EIC maintained the army from the Indian State's own subsidy, so legal ownership of that army could be claimed by the ruler; taking Foreign Policy transferred the right to deploy (war and peace decisions) to the EIC, closing that loophole.

cards.front: What did the annual subsidy paid under a Subsidiary Alliance have to be spent on?
cards.back: Only on maintaining the EIC army stationed in the host State — it was not surplus income the EIC could use freely.

cards.front: How did the Subsidiary Alliance eventually provide grounds for annexing an Indian State?
cards.back: Rising subsidy demands forced rulers to hike taxes; the British Resident then established informal indirect rule; the EIC accused the powerless ruler of maladministration and annexed the State — the starkest case being Nawab Wajid Ali Shah of Awadh, annexed in 1856.

cards.front: How did the EIC acquire territory when an Indian State could not pay the subsidy in cash?
cards.back: It took territory as payment — half of Awadh (Ceded Districts) in 1801 and Berar from Hyderabad in 1853.

cards.front: Which Indian State signed the Subsidiary Alliance first, in 1798, and why?
cards.back: Hyderabad — the Nizam signed to get EIC protection against the Marathas and Mysore.

cards.front: What event forced Peshwa Bajirao II to sign the Treaty of Bassein (December 1802)?
cards.back: He was defeated by Yashwantrao Holkar (avenging his brother's death), fled, and signed the treaty to regain the Peshwaship with EIC support.

cards.front: What territory did Awadh lose in 1801 under the full Subsidiary Alliance, and what was this territory later called?
cards.back: The Doab, Gorakhpur, and Rohilkhand — annexed as permanent subsidy payment; these Ceded Districts were given full province status as the North-West Provinces (NWP) in 1836.

cards.front: What triggered Travancore's Subsidiary Alliance (1805), and why is its timing significant?
cards.back: Travancore signed in exchange for EIC help crushing a Nair troop mutiny over unpaid salaries; it was the last Subsidiary Alliance signed before Wellesley's recall.

cards.front: What territory did the Bhonsle of Nagpur lose to the EIC in the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05)?
cards.back: Significant territory including Orissa (which Bhonsle had taken from Bengal in 1751).

cards.front: Why was Wellesley recalled to London after his tenure as Governor-General (1798–1805)?
cards.back: High war expenditure — empire building was profitable only if wars were short and cheap, and his were neither.

cards.front: What was Mysore's policy of 'Military Fiscalism' under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan?
cards.back: Maximising State revenue as the primary goal — specifically to fund an ever-stronger military, rather than for welfare or administration.

cards.front: What did Tipu Sultan set up to compete directly with the EIC in international trade?
cards.back: A State-owned trading company that entered international trade directly, mirroring the EIC's own mercantilist model.

cards.front: Which three commodities did Tipu Sultan embargo from Mysore-controlled ports to hurt the EIC?
cards.back: Pepper, cardamom, and sandalwood — Malabar being a critical EIC pepper source under Mysore's control since 1766.

cards.front: How did Hyder Ali neutralise the EIC's triple alliance (EIC, Hyderabad, Marathas) before the 1st Anglo-Mysore War?
cards.back: He paid the Marathas 35 lakh rupees to exit, then brought Hyderabad over with 20 lakh rupees plus territorial and political promises.

cards.front: What were the terms of the Treaty of Madras (1769) that ended the 1st Anglo-Mysore War?
cards.back: Both sides returned conquered territories and agreed to a mutual defensive alliance — each promising to assist the other if attacked by a third party.

cards.front: What was the Battle of Pollilur (September 1780) and why was it a shock to the EIC?
cards.back: Hyder Ali annihilated Colonel Baillie's disciplined infantry using iron-cased rockets — one of the worst defeats ever suffered by a European army in India.

cards.front: Who organised the Triple Confederacy of 1780–82 against the EIC, and who were its three members?
cards.back: Nana Fadnis, de-facto ruler of the Peshwa's council, united Marathas, Mysore, and Hyderabad against the EIC.

cards.front: What did Warren Hastings do to break the Triple Confederacy and isolate Mysore?
cards.back: He returned Guntur to Hyderabad (removing their grievance) and signed the Treaty of Salbai (May 1782) with the Marathas, ending the 1st Anglo-Maratha War.

cards.front: What treaty ended the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780–84) and on what terms?
cards.back: Treaty of Mangalore (1784) — both sides returned each other's territories; status quo was maintained.

cards.front: What were the key punitive terms imposed on Tipu Sultan under the Treaty of Seringapatam (1792)?
cards.back: Mysore lost half its kingdom (including Malabar, Dindigul, Baramahal), paid a war fine of 3 crore rupees, and surrendered two of Tipu's own sons as hostages.

cards.front: What happened to Mysore's territory after Tipu Sultan's death in the 4th Anglo-Mysore War (1799)?
cards.back: The best territories (Kanara, Coimbatore, etc.) were split between the EIC and Hyderabad; the remaining core was restored to the Wodeyar dynasty under a Subsidiary Alliance.

cards.front: What four structural reasons explain why Mysore ultimately lost the Anglo-Mysore Wars?
cards.back: 1. No stable alliances. 2. French naval gap — France could not resupply Mysore at sea. 3. War fines drained the treasury. 4. Seringapatam was vulnerable to three-way siege from EIC, Marathas, and Hyderabad.

cards.front: How was Tipu Sultan's religious policy contradictory?
cards.back: He patronised the Sringeri Math and Hindu temples in Mysore, yet carried out forced conversions and destroyed churches and temples during military campaigns in Malabar and Coorg.

cards.front: What mechanism had already drained Carnatic's wealth before the EIC formally annexed it in 1801?
cards.back: The Carnatic Debts — successive Nawabs borrowed from private EIC officials at high interest, pledging Carnatic's jagirs as collateral, which EIC officials then collected revenue from directly.

cards.front: What was the significance of the Battle of Colachel (1741) in Travancore's history?
cards.back: Marthanda Varma decisively defeated the Dutch, enabling him to reorganise Travancore into a centralised revenue-based State — the foundation of its modern power.

cards.front: What was the Kundara Proclamation (January 1809) and who issued it?
cards.back: Velu Thampi Dalawa, Prime Minister of Travancore, issued a public call from Kundara for all Travancoreans to rise against British paramountcy — protesting subsidy demands and EIC interference in internal affairs.

cards.front: Which three agreements completed the EIC's southern consolidation by 1809?
cards.back: The Carnatic annexation (1801), the Travancore Subsidiary Alliance (1805), and the Cochin Subsidiary Alliance (1809).

cards.front: What was the Treaty of Surat (1775) and what did Raghunath Rao give the EIC in exchange for military help?
cards.back: Raghunath Rao promised the EIC Salsette and Bassein, plus revenue from Bharuch and Surat, in exchange for EIC help reclaiming the Peshwaship.

cards.front: What were the key terms of the Treaty of Purandhar (1776) that Warren Hastings negotiated with Nana Fadnis?
cards.back: EIC recognised Madhav Rao II as Peshwa; Raghunath Rao was pensioned off; EIC received Salsette and Bharuch; Marathas barred French presence.

cards.front: Which battle in 1779 ended in a defeat for the EIC and Raghunath Rao during the 1st Anglo-Maratha War?
cards.back: Battle of Wadgaon (near Pune, 1779), where Nana Fadnis, Mahadji Scindhia, and Tukoji Rao Holkar defeated the EIC.

cards.front: Who negotiated the Treaty of Salbai (1782) on behalf of the Marathas, and where was it signed?
cards.back: Mahadji Scindhia negotiated and signed it at Gwalior, ending the 1st Anglo-Maratha War.

cards.front: How did the Treaty of Salbai (1782) differ from the Treaty of Surat (1775) in what the EIC gained?
cards.back: Surat: EIC was promised Salsette, Bassein, and Bharuch revenue. Salbai: EIC kept only Salsette and Bharuch; returned all captured Maratha territory and pensioned off Raghunath Rao.

cards.front: Which single figure had held the Maratha Confederacy together for two decades, and what happened when he died in 1800?
cards.back: Nana Fadnis; his death in 1800 sharply accelerated factionalism within the Confederacy, opening the door for Wellesley's expansion.

cards.front: What triggered Bajirao II's signing of the Treaty of Bassein (December 1802)?
cards.back: Yashwantrao Holkar defeated both Bajirao II and Daulat Rao Scindhia in October 1802; Bajirao II fled and signed a Subsidiary Alliance with the EIC to regain the Peshwaship.

cards.front: What did Arthur Wellesley say about the Battle of Assaye (1803) compared to his European campaigns?
cards.back: He described it as the toughest fight of his entire military career — harder, in his view, than anything he faced against Napoleon in Europe.

cards.front: What territory did Scindhia lose as a result of the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05)?
cards.back: All territory north of the River Yamuna — including Delhi and Agra — and all his territory in Gujarat; he was also forced to sign a Subsidiary Alliance.

cards.front: What was the Policy of Paramountcy (1813–58) introduced by Francis Hastings?
cards.back: EIC declared itself the paramount or supreme power in India, empowered to do anything — including annexation — to protect its interests.

cards.front: How did Appa Sahib exploit the loophole in his Subsidiary Alliance (Treaty of Nagpur, 1816) to secretly rebuild military strength?
cards.back: The SA required disbanding the state army but permitted retainers for internal security; Appa Sahib used this to secretly recruit Arab and Rohilla mercenaries.

cards.front: What is significant about the Battle of Sitabuldi (November 1817) in relation to the Subsidiary Alliance?
cards.back: Appa Sahib had signed the SA in 1816 yet attacked the British Residency in 1817 using Arab mercenaries — exposing that the SA's 'disbanded army' clause was bypassed via a loophole.

cards.front: What was the Battle of Koregaon (1 January 1818) and why is it commemorated?
cards.back: A small EIC force of Mahar soldiers held off a much larger Peshwa army; later commemorated as the Bhima-Koregaon Victory Pillar.

cards.front: What happened to Bajirao II after the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War, and who was his adopted son?
cards.back: Bajirao II was pensioned off to Bithur near Kanpur; his adopted son was Nana Sahib, who later led the Kanpur revolt in 1857.

cards.front: Under which treaty did Holkar of Indore accept a Subsidiary Alliance after the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War?
cards.back: Treaty of Mandsaur (1818), signed after Holkar was decisively defeated at the Battle of Mahidpur.

cards.front: What were the four structural reasons for the Maratha defeat across the Anglo-Maratha Wars?
cards.back: Factionalism; absence of unified command among Scindhia, Holkar, Bhonsle, and Gaikwad; EIC's superior finances; EIC's naval and logistics advantage via the Konkan coast.

cards.front: What territories did Nepal lose under the Treaty of Sugauli (1816) after the Anglo-Nepal War?
cards.back: Nepal lost Kumaon, Garhwal, and the Terai to British India and became a British Protectorate.

cards.front: What was the outcome of the 1st Anglo-Afghan War (1838–42) and who was Auckland's Forward Policy meant to install in Kabul?
cards.back: Catastrophic defeat: 20,000 soldiers dead, Rs 1.5 crore spent, famous retreat from Kabul with only one European survivor; the EIC had tried to install Shah Shuja against ruler Dost Mohammed.

cards.front: What was the Doctrine of Lapse, and who formulated it?
cards.back: Formulated by the Court of Directors of the EIC in 1847: if an Indian ruler died without a biological heir, his state was annexed — adopted heirs were not recognised.

cards.front: Why did the Doctrine of Lapse conflict with Hindu law?
cards.back: Hindu law recognised adopted sons as fully legitimate heirs; the Doctrine refused this, treating adoption as grounds to lapse the state to British control.

cards.front: Which seven states did Dalhousie annex under the Doctrine of Lapse, and between which years?
cards.back: Satara (1848), Sambhalpur (1849), Jaitpur (1849), Baghat (1850), Udaipur (1852), Jhansi (1853–54), Nagpur (1854) — all within seven years.

cards.front: In which present-day state does the Lapse-annexed territory of Baghat lie?
cards.back: Himachal Pradesh — a small hill state near Solan.

cards.front: What was the Inam Commission (1852) and what did it do?
cards.back: A Bombay Presidency body that investigated tax-free land grants (inams) made by earlier Indian rulers; grants with insufficient proof of title were confiscated — seizing around 20,000 estates.

cards.front: Why did Dalhousie refuse Nana Sahib the pension of Peshwa Bajirao II, and what was the consequence?
cards.back: Dalhousie held that adopted sons inherit private wealth, not political titles or state pensions; the refusal made Nana Sahib — based at Bithur — a key leader of the 1857 revolt.

cards.front: How did Dalhousie annex Berar from Hyderabad in 1853?
cards.back: Hyderabad could not pay its Subsidiary Alliance subsidy, so Dalhousie annexed Berar as permanent payment — annexation in lieu of subsidy.

cards.front: On what stated grounds did Dalhousie annex the rest of Awadh in 1856?
cards.back: Maladministration — by 1855 the British Resident had established Indirect Rule, leaving Nawab Wajid Ali Shah with no real power but full responsibility.

cards.front: What happened to Kashmir under the Treaty of Lahore (1846) and the Treaty of Amritsar (1846)?
cards.back: The Lahore Darbar ceded Kashmir to the EIC as part-payment of the war indemnity; the EIC then sold it to Gulab Singh for 75 lakh Nanakshahee rupees, recognising him as Maharaja of Jammu & Kashmir.

cards.front: What were the key terms imposed on Punjab after the 2nd Anglo-Sikh War (1849)?
cards.back: Punjab was annexed from Maharaja Duleep Singh; the Koh-i-Noor diamond was surrendered to the British Crown; Punjab was governed by a Board of Administration (the Lawrence brothers and Charles Mansel).

cards.front: What strategic result did the 2nd Anglo-Burmese War (1852–53) achieve for Britain?
cards.back: Annexation of Lower Burma / Pegu; combined with Arakan and Tenasserim (1824–26), Britain controlled the entire eastern shore of the Bay of Bengal, making it effectively a British lake.

cards.front: Which was the first railway line opened in India, and in what year?
cards.back: The Bombay to Thane line, opened in 1853 under Dalhousie.

cards.front: What was Wood's Despatch (1854) and why is it significant?
cards.back: Sometimes called the 'Magna Carta of Indian Education' — it was a blueprint for mass education covering vernacular elementary schools, universities, and structured education administration, supported and implemented by Dalhousie.

cards.front: What was the Bethune School, who opened it, and what made it notable?
cards.back: India's first successful secular school for girls, opened in Calcutta in 1849 by J.E. Drinkwater Bethune, Law Member of Dalhousie's Council; Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar was closely associated with it.

cards.front: What three modernising infrastructure measures did Dalhousie introduce in 1853–54, and what did each do?
cards.back: Railways (1853): first Bombay–Thane line for army/administration/trade. Telegraph (1853): ~4,000 miles laid across major cities. Post Office Act (1854): uniform half-anna rate from Peshawar to Calcutta.

cards.front: How did the Policy of Paramountcy differ from the Policy of Subordinate Union?
cards.back: Paramountcy (1813–1857): EIC declared itself supreme and could override Indian states' rights. Subordinate Union (after 1858): British Crown absorbed Indian princes as legal subordinates — sovereignty formally vested in the Crown, not just claimed by a company.

cards.front: What did Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 formally do regarding the Doctrine of Lapse?
cards.back: It formally ended the Doctrine of Lapse and pledged that the treaties and rights of Indian rulers would be respected — an explicit reversal of Dalhousie's core annexation policy.

cards.front: Which three major 1857 revolt leaders were directly aggrieved by Dalhousie's annexation policies, and why?
cards.back: Rani Lakshmibai: Jhansi lapsed 1853–54. Nana Sahib: Peshwa pension refused 1851. Bahadur Shah Zafar: Dalhousie sought to end his titular dignity as last Mughal.

cards.front: What was the 'White Man's Burden' and what function did it serve in British imperialism?
cards.back: The foundational belief that Western civilisation was superior, giving Britain a moral duty to civilise the world — the ideological roof justifying all other colonial policies.

cards.front: What was the core argument of Orientalism, and which GG was its most prominent champion?
cards.back: India's ancient past was glorious even if its present was degenerate, so Britain should study Indian tradition and rule India by its own customs — championed by Hastings73-85.

cards.front: Which four institutions did Orientalism produce, who founded each, and in what years?
cards.back: Calcutta Madrasa 1781 (Hastings73-85); Asiatic Society of Bengal 1784 (William Jones); Sanskrit College Banaras 1791 (Jonathan Duncan); Fort William College 1800 (Wellesley98-05).

cards.front: What was the stated purpose of Fort William College (1800), and who founded it?
cards.back: Wellesley98-05 founded it to train newly recruited EIC civil servants in Indian languages and administration.

cards.front: How did the British use the Aryan Invasion Theory to embed a political argument inside Orientalist praise of India?
cards.back: They claimed ancient India's cultural greatness was brought by European migrants — so even while praising India, the British claimed credit for its civilisation.

cards.front: What four measures defined Cornwallis86-93's authoritarian programme for ruling India?
cards.back: All-British senior admin; Rule of Law via Charter Act 1793 codification; Permanent Settlement 1793 in Bengal; Aloof Elite policy barring EIC officials from mixing with Indians.

cards.front: How did Thomas Munro's approach blend Orientalism and Authoritarianism?
cards.back: He governed through Indian forms (Ryotwari Settlement, inspired by ancient direct peasant-revenue collection) but kept total power centralised in EIC hands with no senior Indian roles.

cards.front: What were the three ideologies that replaced Orientalism after 1813, and what was each ideology's core argument?
cards.back: Liberalism: modernise India through western institutions; Utilitarianism: good policy and rule of law maximise benefit; Evangelicalism: change India's religion to transform its society.

cards.front: What were Macaulay's three signature interventions as legal member of the GG's council?
cards.back: Law Commission 1834 (codified western-style laws); Minute on Indian Education 1835 (English medium, Brown Sahibs); Charter Act 1813 reform ending EIC's trade monopoly.

cards.front: What did James Mill argue in his History of British India (1818), and what policy did he push for from the Court of Directors?
cards.back: Mill declared India's great past a myth and argued India needed an effective schoolmaster imposing good governance from above; he pushed for the Law Commission established 1834.

cards.front: Which Evangelical leader influenced the Charter Act 1813 to legalise Christian missionaries entering India?
cards.back: Charles Grant, a member of the Court of Directors and later an MP, was the key Evangelical influence behind the Charter Act 1813.

cards.front: How did the Revolt of 1857 change British racial ideology and reform policy?
cards.back: Reformist impulse collapsed; racial classification shifted from language to physical features marking Indians as an inferior race; social reforms slowed and authoritarianism increased sharply.

cards.front: How did the Forward Policy and the Policy of Ring Fence differ as responses to the Russian threat on the northwest frontier?
cards.back: Forward Policy (Ellenborough, Lytton): push the frontier outward into Afghanistan offensively; Ring Fence: keep strong friendly border states as a defensive buffer around British India.

cards.front: Which GG launched the 2nd Anglo-Afghan War (1878–80) carrying forward the Forward Policy, and what treaty did it produce?
cards.back: Lytton76-80 launched it, producing the Treaty of Gandamak 1879 — a mini-subsidiary alliance giving Britain control of Afghanistan's foreign policy and stationing a British resident in Kabul.

cards.front: What was Imperial Preference, when was it formalised, and what was its operational effect on India?
cards.back: A tariff arrangement formalised at the Ottawa Conference 1932: Empire members gave each other preferential rates, so British goods entered Indian ports at lower tariffs than German, Japanese, or American competitors.

cards.front: In the summary table of ideologies, which four champions and flagship measure are listed for Conservatism (1801–27)?
cards.back: Champions: Munro, Malcolm, Elphinstone, Metcalfe; flagship measures: Ryotwari Settlement and political agencies.

cards.front: What was the Patta system under the Mughals, and what did it protect?
cards.back: A document recording the exact land revenue a Khudkasht owed — a legal safeguard against arbitrary over-extraction by Zamindars.

cards.front: What was the Ijaradari system and who practised it first?
cards.back: Auctioning the right to collect land revenue to the highest bidder (a Revenue Farmer) — introduced by the Mughals when the State needed quick cash, later replicated by the British.

cards.front: Why did the EIC approach Parliament for a bailout by 1772?
cards.back: Rampant official corruption, the 1770 Bengal Famine collapsing land revenue, and heavy army expenses drove the EIC to bankruptcy — Parliament granted £1.4 million at 4% interest, triggering the Regulating Act of 1773.

cards.front: What were the four pillars of the Permanent Settlement of 1793?
cards.back: Zamindars became legal landowners; settlement done with Zamindars; assessment fixed permanently at 10/11 of pre-existing revenue (base year 1789–90); Sunset Clause auctioned land on default.

cards.front: What did the Sunset Clause of the Permanent Settlement mean for a defaulting Zamindar?
cards.back: If he failed to pay land revenue by the pre-set deadline, his land was auctioned to anyone who agreed to pay the required amount — the Zamindar lost his estate.

cards.front: What was the ryot's legal status under the Permanent Settlement, and what did Wellesley's 1799 Regulation VII restore to Zamindars?
cards.back: The ryot became a 'tenant at will' with no legal occupancy rights; Wellesley restored Zamindars' power to seize crops/cattle without a court order, imprison tenants, and raise rents at will.

cards.front: What loophole did Zamindars exploit under the Rent Act of 1859 to deny ryots occupancy rights?
cards.back: Zamindars evicted tenants just before they completed 12 continuous years on a plot, permanently preventing them from gaining occupancy rights — driving the Indigo Revolt and Pabna Agrarian Leagues.

cards.front: What key change in the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 closed the eviction loophole of 1859?
cards.back: Occupancy rights were extended to any tenant who had cultivated different plots in the same village totalling more than 12 years — counting across plots, not just one continuous plot.

cards.front: Who introduced Ryotwari in Madras and when did the first experiment begin?
cards.back: Alexander Read began the first experiment in parts of Madras in 1792; Thomas Munro extended and institutionalised it, firmly re-establishing it as Governor of Madras from 1820–27.

cards.front: What was the Wingate Settlement of 1835, and what problem did it fix?
cards.back: The Bombay Survey System (Wingate and Goldsmid), applied across Bombay Deccan by 1847, replaced R.K. Pringle's excessive 55% demand with a fair assessment fixed at a reasonable annual amount for 30 years.

cards.front: What cap did the Madras Rules of 1855/1864 place on Ryotwari land revenue?
cards.back: A maximum of 50% of net produce / rental value, fixed for 30 years — introduced after the Madras Torture Commission Report (1855) exposed severe oppression of ryots.

cards.front: Who designed the Mahalwari Settlement, and what law enacted it?
cards.back: Holt Mackenzie's recommendations were enacted through Regulation VII of 1822; R.M. Bird revised the system in 1833, fixing assessment at 66% of rental value for 30 years.

cards.front: What was a Mahal, and who was the Lambardar?
cards.back: A Mahal was a community at the village, estate or district level; the Lambardar was its representative who acted as the interface between the Mahal and the State for land revenue.

cards.front: Why did the summary settlement of Awadh in 1856 fuel the 1857 revolt?
cards.back: Revenue was fixed without field surveys (too time-consuming), producing unjust demands for many ryots and widespread landlessness — added to the earlier crushing of Taluqdars (1801–22) and unjust extraction.

cards.front: How did British cash-revenue demands cause the commercialisation of Indian agriculture?
cards.back: Ryots needed cash to pay revenue, so they shifted from food crops (rice, wheat, millets) to cash crops (indigo, cotton, opium, jute, sugarcane) — reducing food-grain reserves and feeding the late-19th-century famines.

cards.front: How did the three British land-revenue systems differ in landowner, settlement party, assessment rate, and region?
cards.back: PS (1793): Zamindar owns, settled with Zamindar, fixed forever at 10/11 revenue, Bengal/Orissa/Bihar/Benaras/N.Madras. Ryotwari (1801/1820+): Ryot owns, settled directly with ryot, 50% net rental value 30 yrs, SCAM-B. Mahalwari (1822/1833): Mostly ryot (hybrid), settled with Mahal via Lambardar, 66% rental value 30 yrs, CUP.

cards.front: Why did Cornwallis choose Zamindars as landowners while Munro chose ryots?
cards.back: Cornwallis (English) believed in landlordism and wanted agrarian capitalists like England's landed gentry; Munro (Scottish) believed in the yeoman farmer and argued ancient India had no intermediaries between State and cultivator.

cards.front: What did the Regulating Act of 1773 do to the Governor of Bengal Presidency?
cards.back: Elevated him to Governor-General of Bengal Presidency — a higher authority over the Governors of Bombay and Madras in matters of war and peace.

cards.front: Who was the first Chief Justice of the Calcutta Supreme Court, and when was he appointed?
cards.back: Sir Elijah Impey, appointed in 1774 — the court itself having been established under the Regulating Act of 1773.

cards.front: What were 'puisne judges' as used in the Regulating Act of 1773?
cards.back: Junior judges — three of them sat alongside one Chief Justice in the Supreme Court at Calcutta.

cards.front: What did the Amending Act of 1781 (Bengal Judicature Act) settle about the Calcutta Supreme Court's jurisdiction?
cards.back: SC heard all cases within Calcutta, all cases of British subjects in Bengal Presidency (excluding EIC officials' official acts), and all EIC property cases at Fort William.

cards.front: What was the Board of Control created by Pitt's India Act (1784), and who sat on it?
cards.back: A six-member British State body to superintend EIC's political affairs — comprising one Secretary of State (President), the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and four Privy Council members.

cards.front: What did Pitt's India Act (1784) explicitly declare about conquest in India?
cards.back: "Conquest in India is repugnant to the wish, policy and honour of this nation" — banning imperial expansion in response to costly recent wars.

cards.front: What two changes did the Amending Act of 1786 make to Pitt's India Act (1784)?
cards.back: Gave GG a veto over his council in extraordinary circumstances, and permitted the same person to hold both GG and Commander-in-Chief posts simultaneously.

cards.front: Who were the first four Governors-General / Viceroys, in order of designation change?
cards.back: Warren Hastings = 1st GG(Bengal) 1773; William Bentinck = 1st GG(India) 1833; Charles Canning = 1st Viceroy & GG 1858; C. Rajagopalachari = 1st Indian GG 1948.

cards.front: What did the Charter Act of 1793 establish about the appointment of EIC's Principal Servants?
cards.back: They were to be appointed by the EIC only after approval of the Crown — covering GG, Governors, Commander-in-Chief, and Councillors.

cards.front: What did the Charter Act of 1793 mandate about codification of law in Bengal?
cards.back: A code of all regulations governing Bengal — covering rights of persons and property — was to be framed, and all laws printed in vernacular languages.

cards.front: Which trade monopolies did the EIC retain after the Charter Act of 1813 ended its general India monopoly?
cards.back: Tea, Opium trade, and trade with China were retained as exceptions to the 1813 liberalisation.

cards.front: What education provision did the Charter Act of 1813 introduce?
cards.back: EIC was mandated to spend Rs 1 lakh per annum on education, alongside allowing Christian Missionaries to enter India with a licence from CoD or BoC.

cards.front: What change did the Charter Act of 1833 make to the Governor-General's designation, and who was the first holder of the new title?
cards.back: GG(Bengal) was elevated to GG(India); William Bentinck, already in office, became the first GG of India in 1833.

cards.front: Who was the first Law Member added to GG(India)'s council under the Charter Act of 1833, and what was his nationality?
cards.back: Thomas Macaulay — an Englishman; no Indian was appointed Law Member under this Act.

cards.front: What racial equality promise did the Charter Act of 1833 make regarding EIC service?
cards.back: "No person to be deprived of chance to enter EIC service on grounds of religion, race, birth or colour" — also opening Uncovenanted Civil Services to Indians.

cards.front: How did the Charter Act of 1853 change how Civil Service appointments were made?
cards.back: Introduced a competitive Civil Services Examination — the first held in London in 1855 — ending EIC's patronage power to independently appoint its officials.

cards.front: Who was the first Lieutenant Governor of Bengal, and who appointed him?
cards.back: Frederick James Halliday, appointed by Dalhousie in 1854 under the power the Charter Act of 1853 granted the GG to appoint a LG for Bengal.

cards.front: What body replaced the Board of Control under the Government of India Act (1858), and who headed it?
cards.back: The Council of India (India Council) — headed by the Secretary of State for India, with 15 members, seven drawn from EIC's Court of Directors.

cards.front: What four commitments did Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 specifically make?
cards.back: Disclaimed intention to annex Indian States; placed administration under the Crown; promised religious non-interference and race/creed-blind public service; granted amnesty to most 1857 participants.

cards.front: What did Warren Hastings do in 1772 to end the Dual Government in Bengal?
cards.back: He assumed direct administration of both Diwani (civil/revenue) and Nizamat (law and order), ending the arrangement where the Nawab retained Nizamat.

cards.front: What was the Gentoo Code (1776) and what does the word 'Gentoo' come from?
cards.back: An English translation of Hindu law codified by 11 Pandits in 1775; 'Gentoo' came from the Portuguese 'Gentios', a derogatory term for Hindus used by Christian Europeans.

cards.front: What is Anglo-Muhammadan law and how long was it in use?
cards.back: A hybrid criminal code combining Islamic law with British modifications, applied from Cornwallis's 1793 reforms until the Indian Penal Code 1860 — roughly 70 years.

cards.front: What three British modifications did Cornwallis make to Islamic criminal law?
cards.back: Replaced the weapon-based murder rule with intent (mens rea); abolished 'blood money' (Diyat) pardons by victims' heirs; outlawed mutilation, replacing it with hard labour of 7–14 years.

cards.front: Why did Cornwallis strip the District Collector of judicial powers in 1793?
cards.back: His Permanent Settlement 1793 created a new zamindar class needing secure property rights — a revenue officer could not fairly judge disputes arising from his own tax decisions.

cards.front: How did Bentinck change the language of courts in 1835?
cards.back: He replaced Persian with vernaculars in lower courts and English in higher courts, backed by Act XXIX of 1837, causing anxiety among Muslim elites who had relied on Persian for administrative careers.

cards.front: What three courts were merged to form the Calcutta High Court in 1862?
cards.back: The Sadar Diwani Adalat, the Sadar Nizamat Adalat, and the Calcutta Supreme Court — finally ending the dual-track system of separate courts for Indians and British.

cards.front: What distinguished the Covenanted Civil Service (CCS) from the Uncovenanted Civil Service (UCS)?
