cards.back: CCS officers signed a formal contract with the EIC's Court of Directors in London before sailing; UCS officers were hired locally in India by the GG or provincial governors at lower pay.

cards.front: What specific innovation did Cornwallis introduce for civil service promotions — and what did he NOT change?
cards.back: He introduced strict seniority for promotions once inside; he did NOT introduce merit-based entry — recruitment remained patronage-based nomination until Charter Act 1853.

cards.front: Who was the first Indian to clear the Covenanted Civil Service examination, and in what year?
cards.back: Satyendranath Tagore (brother of Rabindranath Tagore) cleared the CCS exam in 1864.

cards.front: What was the Statutory Civil Services Act 1878 and who introduced it?
cards.back: Viceroy Lytton76-80 created lateral entry by nomination for loyal elite Indians to CCS-reserved posts — a bypass of the exam that avoided raising age limits or holding the exam in India.

cards.front: What did the Aitchison Commission 1887 recommend, and what is the key exam-trap about its implementation?
cards.back: It recommended three tiers — ICS, PCS, Subordinate — implemented in 1892 by executive order under Lansdowne88-94, NOT by the Indian Councils Act 1892 (a classic exam trap).

cards.front: What was the Daroga system introduced by Cornwallis in 1793?
cards.back: Each district was divided into thanas of 30 square miles, each under an Indian Daroga supervised by the European District Magistrate — replacing the police powers of zamindars.

cards.front: Why did the British adopt the Irish Constabulary model for Indian policing?
cards.back: It was a centralised, quasi-military force proven in Ireland since 1787 for suppressing political agitation — the British were building a political control mechanism, not primarily a crime-prevention force.

cards.front: Who introduced the Irish Constabulary model in Sindh and when — and who is wrongly credited in many guidebooks?
cards.back: Charles Napier set up the Sindh Police on this model in 1843 after conquest; M.H. Court (not Napier) chaired the 1st Police Commission 1860 that nationalised the model — a common UPSC trap.

cards.front: What did the Fraser Commission (1902–03) create for the police, and what did it refuse to do?
cards.back: It unified superior officers into the Imperial Police (IP) cadre and created the CID in every province; it refused to open the IP to Indians, preserving racial superiority at the senior level.

cards.front: How did the District Collector and District Magistrate roles differ under British administration?
cards.back: DC: revenue collection, land records, taxes — descended from Mughal Diwani function; DM: criminal administration and law and order — descended from Mughal Nizamat/Faujdari function; usually the same person.

cards.front: Which codified laws emerged from Macaulay's Law Commission (set up 1834) and when were they enacted?
cards.back: Civil Procedure Code 1859, Indian Penal Code 1860, and Criminal Procedure Code 1861 — codification was substantially complete by 1837 but implemented only after the 1857 revolt.

cards.front: Why is Ram Mohan Roy called the Father of Modern India?
cards.back: He was the first to grasp that social reform required religious reform, and the first to synthesise Indian tradition with Western modernity.

cards.front: What was Ram Mohan Roy's primary intellectual concern about Hindu religion?
cards.back: He argued from the Upanishads themselves that authentic Hinduism is monotheistic, pointing to one God — not polytheistic.

cards.front: What caused the 1866 split in the Brahmo Samaj?
cards.back: Keshab Chandra Sen's faction wanted to break from Hinduism; Debendranath Tagore's faction wanted to stay within it — producing Brahmo Samaj of India (Sen) and Adi Brahmo Samaj (Tagore).

cards.front: What was the major catch of the Brahmo Marriages Act of 1872?
cards.back: Bride and groom had to formally leave Hinduism first — a condition that severely limited the Act's real-world impact on inter-caste and widow remarriages.

cards.front: What personal act by Keshab Chandra Sen in 1878 fractured his Brahmo Samaj of India?
cards.back: He married off his own minor daughter — directly contradicting his public campaign against child marriage — leading to formation of the Sadharan Brahmo Samaj (1878).

cards.front: What legislation abolished Sati in 1829, and what was it formally called?
cards.back: The Bengal Sati Regulation (Regulation XVII, 1829) under Bentinck, making Sati punishable as culpable homicide.

cards.front: What was the Dharma Sabha (1830) and why was it formed?
cards.back: An orthodox Hindu organisation founded by Radhakanta Deb specifically to oppose the abolition of Sati; it petitioned the Privy Council in London to overturn Regulation XVII — the petition was rejected.

cards.front: What was Jyotirao Phule's Satyashodhak Samaj (1873), and what companion publication did he start?
cards.back: The Truth-Seekers' Society, which challenged orthodoxy and the caste system; he also started the newspaper Din Bandhu (1877) for the oppressed classes.

cards.front: What did Phule's Gulamgiri (1873) argue, and to whom did he dedicate it?
cards.back: It equated the condition of Shudras and Ati-Shudras with African American slaves; Phule dedicated it to American abolitionists.

cards.front: What legislative victory did Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar achieve in 1856, and what was the first remarriage date?
cards.back: The Hindu Widow Remarriage Act of 26 July 1856 under Dalhousie; the first remarriage under the Act took place on 7 December 1856.

cards.front: What is the founding date, place, and motto of the Arya Samaj?
cards.back: Founded 10 April 1875 in Bombay; motto: 'Krinvanto Vishvam Aryam' — Make this world noble.

cards.front: What is Satyarth Prakash (1875), and why did Dayanand write it in Hindi rather than Sanskrit?
cards.back: The foundational text of the Arya Samaj by Maharishi Dayanand; written in Hindi so it could reach the masses rather than only the learned.

cards.front: What was the Arya Samaj's Shuddhi Movement?
cards.back: A programme to bring back those who had voluntarily or involuntarily converted to Islam or Christianity — purification for those who sought to return, not forced re-conversion under Dayananda himself.

cards.front: Where and when did Swami Vivekananda represent Hinduism on the world stage, and what did he argue?
cards.back: At the Parliament of Religions in Chicago, 1893; he argued that Western materialism and Indian spiritualism must come together for the welfare of mankind.

cards.front: What was the Ramakrishna Mission (1897), and what was Vivekananda's core equation behind it?
cards.back: Founded by Vivekananda to spread Vedanta and undertake social service; grounded in his equation: service of Jiva is worship of Shiva — social service is a spiritual act.

cards.front: What institution did Sir Syed Ahmed Khan found in 1875, and what rival body did he set up in 1886?
cards.back: Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh (1875), the heart of the Aligarh Movement; and the Mohammadan Educational Congress (1886) as a deliberate rival to the INC.

cards.front: What was Narayana Guru's first temple consecration act (1888), and what did he say to upper-caste critics?
cards.back: He consecrated a Shiva idol at Aruvippuram; to critics who said a lower-caste man had no right, he replied: 'This is not a Brahmin's Shiva. This is an Ezhava's Shiva.'

cards.front: What organisation did Narayana Guru found in 1903, and for what purpose?
cards.back: The Shri Narayana Dharma Paripalana Yogam (SNDP), for the social, educational, and economic upliftment of the Ezhava community and lower castes broadly.

cards.front: What was India's first newspaper, when was it launched, and why was it shut down?
cards.back: Bengal Gazette (English), launched in Calcutta in 1780 by James Augustus Hicky; shut down in 1782 by Warren Hastings for criticising the British.

cards.front: What was the Amrita Bazar Patrika's famous act to escape the Vernacular Press Act (1878)?
cards.back: It converted overnight from Bengali to English in 1878, moving itself outside the Act's jurisdiction.

cards.front: Which two newspapers did Ram Mohan Roy found, in which languages, and in which years?
cards.back: Sambad Kaumudi (Bengali, 1821) to advocate social reforms; Mirat-ul-Akhbar (Persian, 1822) to promote liberal ideas — the latter closed by John Adams's Licensing Regulations of 1823.

cards.front: Who was Henry Vivian Derozio, and what did Young Bengal's 1838 Society for Acquisition of General Knowledge achieve?
cards.back: A Eurasian teacher at Hindu College, Calcutta (died December 1831); the Society debated Western sciences and social reforms but built no mass movement and had no engagement with religious sentiment.

cards.front: What was the Farming System of 1772 in Bengal, and who collected land revenue under it?
cards.back: Land revenue collection was auctioned to the highest bidder — a revenue farmer — who extracted rent from peasants under the District Collector's supervision.

cards.front: What occupancy right did the Rent Act of 1859 grant ryots, and why was it ineffective?
cards.back: Ryots who cultivated the same plot continuously for over twelve years earned the right not to be arbitrarily evicted, but implementation in Bengal was ineffective and exploitation continued.

cards.front: How did the indigo contract system trap Bengal ryots in permanent debt?
cards.back: Planters made ryots take an upfront loan, then bought back their indigo far below market rate, keeping them perpetually indebted with no legal escape.

cards.front: What did the Lex Loci Act of 1850 do, and why did it anger many peasants and traders?
cards.back: It gave converts to another religion the right of inheritance; many saw it as British interference in religious life and a threat to their faith.

cards.front: What three categories did the Indian Forests Act 1878 create, and which Viceroy passed it?
cards.back: Reserved Forests, Protected Forests, and Village Forests — passed under Viceroy Lytton (1876–80).

cards.front: What was the legal masterstroke of the Indian Forests Act 1878 regarding customary rights?
cards.back: It redefined customary community rights as privileges granted by the colonial state — privileges that could be taxed, restricted, or revoked at any time.

cards.front: How did Reserved Forests differ from Protected Forests under the 1878 Act?
cards.back: Reserved: everything prohibited unless specifically permitted, all traditional community rights extinguished. Protected: everything permitted unless specifically prohibited, state could close sections over time.

cards.front: Why did the British need absolute control over forests in the 1870s?
cards.back: The railway boom required enormous timber for sleepers — each mile of track needed roughly 2,000 wooden sleepers of durable wood such as teak, sal, and deodar.

cards.front: How did the Abkari (Excise) Administration dispossess tribal communities of their brewing traditions?
cards.back: The colonial state claimed a monopoly over liquor manufacture and sale, criminalised traditional brewing, and auctioned tapping rights to contractors who raised prices steeply.

cards.front: Who were the two religious groups in the Sanyasi-Fakir rebellion, and what united them despite different faiths?
cards.back: The Dasnami Sanyasis (Hindu peasants and traders) and the Madari Fakirs (Muslim peasants); identical economic grievances — high revenue, high rents, and EIC trade monopoly — united them.

cards.front: What was the Faraizi movement's most powerful slogan, and who gave it?
cards.back: Dudu Mian declared that land belongs to God, therefore any rent or tax on land is ungodly — making economic resistance a religious obligation.

cards.front: What physical identity did Titu Mir's followers adopt, and what specific tax triggered their revolt?
cards.back: They adopted a distinct beard and dress as markers of resistance; the immediate trigger was a tax on beards levied by the local zamindar.

cards.front: How did British annexation after the Third Anglo-Mysore War transform the Moplahs' legal status in Malabar?
cards.back: The British recognised only Janmies as legal landowners, stripping Moplahs of all customary rights and reducing them overnight to exploited tenants with no legal standing.

cards.front: What political outcome did the Santhal Rebellion of 1855 produce, despite being crushed militarily?
cards.back: A separate administrative unit — Santhal Parganas — was created with formal protections for tribal culture and restrictions on transfer of Santhal land to non-tribals.

cards.front: What did the Santhals call their homeland, and what name did they give to outsider zamindars and moneylenders?
cards.back: They called their homeland Damini-i-koh (the skirts of the hills) and called outsiders Dikus.

cards.front: What was the Kol Rebellion's notable restraint in targeting, and what had caused their dispossession?
cards.back: The Kols targeted the property of outsider moneylenders called Suds, not their lives; dispossession came when the Raja of Chhotanagpur farmed out tribal lands to these outsiders.

cards.front: Why did Birsa Munda choose Christmas 1899 to launch the Ulugulan?
cards.back: It was a deliberate act of political symbolism — rising against British power on the most sacred day of the religion missionaries were using to erode Munda identity.

cards.front: What did Alluri Sitarama Raju conclude after the withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922, and what happened to him?
cards.back: He concluded India could be liberated only by force, re-initiated the Fituri (violent rebellion), was captured, and was executed in 1924.

cards.front: How does the chapter define the Revolt of 1857?
cards.back: A sepoy mutiny combined with a civil rebellion — two streams that flowed together into one of the most significant events in the history of British rule in India.

cards.front: Who fired the opening shot of the Revolt of 1857, and where?
cards.back: Mangal Pandey, a sepoy of the 34th Bengal Native Infantry, fired at European officers at Barrackpur near Calcutta on 29 March 1857.

cards.front: What happened at Meerut on 10 May 1857?
cards.back: Sepoys mutinied, then marched to Delhi and proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar — the last Mughal emperor — as Emperor of Hindustan.

cards.front: What was the highest rank an Indian sepoy could reach in the British Indian Army, and what was its pay?
cards.back: Subedar, worth only 60–70 rupees a month — far below European soldiers' pay.

cards.front: What specific economic measure in 1856 angered Bengal Army sepoys on top of already-low pay?
cards.back: The British cut sepoy salaries and abolished the regional service allowance, which was both an economic blow and a religious insult for upper-caste men.

cards.front: Why was the Enfield rifle cartridge the immediate trigger for the sepoy mutiny?
cards.back: Rumours spread that the cartridges — which replaced the Brown Bess musket and had to be bitten before loading — were greased with cow and pig fat.

cards.front: Why did the revolt begin specifically in the Bengal Army rather than the Madras or Bombay armies?
cards.back: Upper-caste identity had been most carefully preserved in the Bengal Army, and the ratio of British to Indian soldiers was lowest there.

cards.front: Which rebel leader led each major centre of the Revolt of 1857?
cards.back: Nana Sahib → Kanpur; Begum Hazrat Mahal → Lucknow; Khan Bahadur Khan Rohilla → Bareilly; Rani Lakshmi Bai → Jhansi; Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah → Faizabad/Awadh; Kunwar Singh → Jagdishpur, Bihar; Tantia Tope → Nana Sahib's military commander.

cards.front: How did Rani Lakshmi Bai die, and what did her death represent?
cards.back: She died in battle at Gwalior on 17–18 June 1858, becoming one of the most celebrated symbols of the revolt.

cards.front: What was Tantia Tope's fate after the fall of Kanpur and Jhansi?
cards.back: He waged a prolonged guerrilla campaign across central India, was eventually betrayed by his associate Man Singh, captured, and hanged in April 1859.

cards.front: What happened to Bahadur Shah Zafar after the fall of Delhi?
cards.back: He was captured, tried, and exiled to Rangoon (Burma), where he died in 1862 — ending his days as a prisoner far from his ancestors' empire.

cards.front: What was the Lex Loci Act of 1850, and why did it fuel religious fear ahead of 1857?
cards.back: A law giving inheritance rights to those who converted to Christianity — effectively incentivising conversion and feeding fears of forced religious change.

cards.front: Which regions stayed out of the Revolt of 1857, and what was the common reason?
cards.back: Ryotwari areas (Sindh, Assam, Madras, Bombay), Punjab, and Bengal — their populations or zamindars had economically benefited under British rule and had little motive to rebel.

cards.front: What is V.D. Savarkar's characterisation of 1857, and when did he publish it?
cards.back: In his 1909 book, Savarkar called it the Indian War of Independence, fought for Swadharma and Swaraj.

cards.front: What legislation ended East India Company rule after 1857, and what was its key provision?
cards.back: The Government of India Act, 1858, made Queen Victoria sovereign of India and established direct Crown rule over British India.

cards.front: What police reform directly resulted from the British security failure exposed by 1857?
cards.back: The 1st Police Commission (1860), led by M.H. Court under Canning, produced the Police Act, 1861, creating a provincial police structure from Inspector General down to Sub-Inspector at the thana.

cards.front: How did the British use the ICS eligibility age to exclude Indian candidates after 1857?
cards.back: The maximum age was deliberately set at 19–23 — low enough that most Indian students, finishing education later than British peers, would be too old before they were ready.

cards.front: What was the Peel Commission, and what soldier ratio did it prescribe for the Bengal Army?
cards.back: The Royal Commission on Reorganisation of the Indian Army (1858–59), headed by Major-General Jonathan Peel, prescribed 1 British soldier for every 2 Indian soldiers in the Bengal Army (1:2).

cards.front: In what two key ways did post-1857 peasant revolts differ from earlier uprisings?
cards.back: Peasants used British courts and legal institutions rather than only weapons, and the Western Educated Middle Class began actively championing peasant causes.

cards.front: In what year did the EIC begin promoting Indigo cultivation in Bengal, and to whom did it give preferential loans?
cards.back: 1788; the EIC gave loans to ten European planters rather than to local zamindars.

cards.front: What was the Ryoti System of Indigo cultivation, and what three conditions bound the ryot under it?
cards.back: Planters leased land from zamindars and contracted ryots to: grow Indigo on at least 25% of their land, accept low-interest loans and seeds, and sell the harvested Indigo back to the planter.

cards.front: What play exposed Indigo planter oppression in 1860, who wrote it, and who translated it into English?
cards.back: Neel Darpan (Blue Mirror) by DeenBandhu Mitra; Bengali poet Michael Madhusudhan Datta translated it into English.

cards.front: Who published the English translation of Neel Darpan, and what was his punishment?
cards.back: Christian missionary James Long published it; he was convicted of libel, fined Rs 1,000 (paid by Kaliprasanna Sinha), and imprisoned for one month.

cards.front: What ruling did the Indigo Commission of 1860 make regarding ryots and future contracts?
cards.back: Ryots had to honour existing contracts but were free to refuse all future Indigo contracts.

cards.front: What was the Tinkathia System, and where did it operate after Indigo cultivation shifted out of Bengal?
cards.back: A system identical to the Ryoti System but requiring the ryot to grow Indigo on 3/20th of his land; it operated in Bihar and was ended by the Champaran Agrarian Act of 1918.

cards.front: What ended natural Indigo cultivation more decisively than peasant resistance, and when?
cards.back: In 1897 the German company BASF developed synthetic indigo, which was cheaper and more consistent, collapsing global demand for the natural product.

cards.front: What three grievances drove the Pabna Agrarian League movement of 1873?
cards.back: Zamindars violated the occupancy rights granted by the Rent Act of 1859, raised rents illegally, and collected unauthorised extra cesses called Abwabs.

cards.front: Which leader spread the Pabna Agrarian Leagues beyond Pabna district, and what legislation eventually gave ryots genuine relief?
cards.back: Ishan Chandra Roy replicated the movement in neighbouring districts; the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885, passed after Ripon's Rent Commission of 1880, brought genuine relief.

cards.front: What was the Deccan ryots' specific method of protest during the 1873–74 Maharashtra riots, and why did they target that object?
cards.back: They burned debt bonds rather than attacking moneylenders personally, showing awareness that the bond — not the individual — was the instrument of their oppression.

cards.front: What did the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870) achieve, and with which reformer was it associated?
cards.back: Associated with M.G. Ranade, it collected 17,000 signatures and convinced the government that land confiscation must be the last resort for recovering Land Revenue arrears.

cards.front: What act did the British pass in 1879 in response to the Deccan agrarian unrest, and what did it provide?
cards.back: The Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act of 1879, which protected ryots against loss of land due to indebtedness and regulated interest rates.

cards.front: Who led the Namdhari (Kuka) revolt in Punjab, and what was his fate in 1872?
cards.back: Baba Ram Singh, head of the Namdhari Sect, led the revolt and was exiled to Burma in 1872.

cards.front: Why did the British quietly withdraw the Punjab land-canal bill despite having suppressed the no-tax agitation?
cards.back: Post-1857 the Indian Army was heavily recruited from Punjab's Sikh community, and peasant disaffection risked spreading to the army — a risk the British could not afford.

cards.front: What single pattern runs through the Bengal, Maharashtra, and Punjab peasant revolts after 1857?
cards.back: In every case peasants organised formally — leagues, petitions, court cases — and sections of the Western Educated Middle Class (journalists, lawyers, reformers) amplified their cause.

cards.front: Which organisation was the first major voluntary organisation in India, and when was it founded?
cards.back: The British Indian Association [BrIA1851], founded in Calcutta in 1851.

cards.front: Who was the first president of the British Indian Association (1851)?
cards.back: Radhakanta Deb.

cards.front: What was Dwarkanath Tagore's earlier organisation (1838), and how did it differ from the British Indian Association?
cards.back: The Landholders' Society (1838); unlike the BrIA, it included many non-official Anglo-Indians, making it less purely Indian in character.

cards.front: Which three regional associations were all formed in 1851–52, and what immediate event prompted their founding?
cards.back: British Indian Association (1851), Bombay Association (1852), and Madras Native Association (1852) — all formed as the British Parliament deliberated on the Charter Act of 1853.

cards.front: What did the three early associations (BrIA, Bombay, Madras) mean when they complained of 'un-British rule'?
cards.back: They argued exploitation was a departure from British governance's own standards of justice — they opposed bad administration, not colonialism itself.

cards.front: How did the 'common grievances' of the 1851–52 associations differ from their 'elite personal interests'?
cards.back: Common: high taxes, expensive/incompetent administration, neglect of education and public works. Elite: opposition to salt and opium monopolies.

cards.front: What did the Census of 1921 reveal about literacy in India, despite the Wood's Dispatch (1854) and Hunter Commission (1882–83)?
cards.back: Only 8% overall literacy and a mere 2% female literacy — confirming mass education had remained neglected.

cards.front: Which social groups dominated early INM leadership, and which group was comparatively underrepresented?
cards.back: Upper-caste Marathis, Tamilians, and Bengalis of the Presidency Towns dominated; Muslims were comparatively underrepresented.

cards.front: How large was India's newspaper landscape by 1875, and what was the combined readership?
cards.back: Over 400 newspapers in English and vernacular languages, with a combined readership of more than 1.5 lakh.

cards.front: During whose viceroyalty (with tenure years) did measures like the Vernacular Press Act, the Arms Act, and the Delhi Durbar of 1877 antagonise educated Indian opinion?
cards.back: Viceroy Lytton76-80 (1876–1880).

cards.front: Which British political party's victory in 1880 brought Lord Ripon to India, and what was his tenure?
cards.back: Gladstone's Liberal Party; Ripon served as Viceroy from 1880 to 1884 [Ripon80-84].

cards.front: What was the stated goal of Ripon's Local Self-Government Resolution/Act of 1882?
cards.back: To train Indians in the practice of self-government.

cards.front: Who drafted the Ilbert Bill (1883), and what privilege did it seek to end?
cards.back: Law Member C.P. Ilbert drafted it; it sought to end the privilege by which a Briton in rural India could not be tried before an Indian judge.

cards.front: What was the key compromise in the final version of the Ilbert Bill after European protests forced its withdrawal and amendment?
cards.back: The final version required a mixed jury in any case involving a Briton.

cards.front: How did the post-1870 WEMC associations differ from the earlier landed-class associations of 1851–52?
cards.back: 1851–52 bodies: led by conservative educated landlords, regional lobbies, petitioned on elite interests. Post-1870 WEMC bodies: led by young professionals, politically minded, challenged older bodies and gradually replaced them as the principal voice of Indian opinion.

cards.front: Which legislative act allowed more Indians as members of the Councils, enabling WEMC associations to use them as platforms for criticism?
cards.back: The Indian Councils Act of 1892 (ICA1892).

cards.front: Where and when was the Indian National Congress founded, and who was its first President?
cards.back: Founded in Bombay in December 1885; its first President was Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee.

cards.front: What role did A.O. Hume play in founding the INC, and what was his background?
cards.back: He was a retired British civil servant who toured India in the early 1880s and persuaded leaders in Bombay, Madras, and Calcutta to gather for a common conference.

cards.front: What is the 'Safety Valve Theory' of the INC's founding?
cards.back: The claim that Hume founded the INC as a deliberate British strategy to let the educated elite air grievances peacefully and prevent a violent mass uprising.

cards.front: Who first put forward the Safety Valve Theory, and in what work?
cards.back: William Wedderburn, in his 1913 biography of Hume — written nearly four decades after the supposed events.

cards.front: What three arguments disprove the Safety Valve Theory as given in the chapter?
cards.back: The seven secret volumes were never found; Dufferin dismissed Moderates as a 'microscopic minority of Babus'; and Dufferin feared the INC would become an Irish Home Rule League, not a safe outlet.

cards.front: How did Viceroy Dufferin (1884–88) actually view the Indian National Congress at its founding?
cards.back: With suspicion — he asked the Bombay Governor to stay alert and feared the INC could grow into a movement like the Irish Home Rule League.

cards.front: What organisation did Surendranath Banerjea lead, and what parallel body did he convene before the INC?
cards.back: He led the Indian Association (1876) and convened the Indian National Conference, which met in 1883 and 1885 before merging into the INC in 1886.

cards.front: What practical reason did Gokhale give in 1913 for why having a British founder was valuable for the INC?
cards.back: The British would never have allowed an all-India organisation to be formed under Indian leadership; Hume gave the INC protective cover in its early years.

cards.front: What were at least three all-India political agitations Indian organisations ran before 1885?
cards.back: Protests against the Income Tax (1868), a campaign for Indianisation of Civil Services (1877), support for the Ilbert Bill (1883–84), and opposition to the Vernacular Press Act (1878), among others.

cards.front: What model did Hume want the INC to follow, and what role did he personally hold in it?
cards.back: He wanted it to function like 'His Majesty's Opposition' — a legitimate channel of dissent; he served as General Secretary, not President.

cards.front: Who was the first non-Indian President of the INC, at which session, and what was his profession?
cards.back: George Yule presided over the Allahabad Session in 1888; he was a merchant and founder of the Agency House 'Andrew Yule & Company' in Calcutta.

cards.front: Who was the second non-Indian President of the INC, and in which years did he serve in that role?
cards.back: William Wedderburn, who served as INC President in 1889 and again in 1910.

cards.front: Who was the third non-Indian President of the INC, at which session, and who personally invited him?
cards.back: Alfred Webb presided over the Madras Session of 1894; he was invited personally by Dadabhai Naoroji.

cards.front: How did Hume, Wedderburn, and Jardine each serve the INC at its co-founding in 1885?
cards.back: Hume: General Secretary and chief organiser. Wedderburn: co-founder, ex-Secretary to Bombay Government. Jardine: co-founder, former Chief Secretary and Judge of the Bombay High Court.

cards.front: What two reform causes did Alfred Webb champion beyond his INC presidency?
cards.back: He supported Britain's first anti-racist journal and opposed the opium trade into China.

cards.front: What post did Hume hold before founding the INC, and which viceroy dismissed him and why?
cards.back: He was Secretary of the Department of Revenue, Agriculture & Commerce; Viceroy Lytton (1876–80) dismissed him for opposing heavy expenditure on the Afghan War (1878–80).

cards.front: Which Secretary of State described British Indian governance as 'despotism controlled from home'?
cards.back: Charles Wood — and this principle remained the operating basis of British Indian governance right until 1947.

cards.front: What two laws of 1861 together overhauled the entire British Indian State machinery in one year?
cards.back: Indian Councils Act, 1861 (legislature & executive) and the Indian High Courts Act, 1861 (judiciary).

cards.front: What is the 'expanded-council model' introduced by the Indian Councils Act, 1861?
cards.back: The VEC wore two hats: sitting alone for executive work it was the VEC; joined by additional members for law-making it became the ILC.

cards.front: Which Act abolished the expanded-council model and replaced it with a fully bicameral Central Legislature (Council of State + Central Legislative Assembly)?
cards.back: Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms).

cards.front: What was the Portfolio System introduced by Canning (1856–62) in 1859, and what did the Indian Councils Act, 1861 do with it?
cards.back: Allocating specific departments to individual VEC members whose decisions were final (subject to Viceroy's veto); ICA 1861 gave it legal recognition.

cards.front: Why was a 5th Ordinary Member (Finance Member) added to the VEC by the Indian Councils Act, 1861?
cards.back: The 1857 revolt left British India heavily in debt, requiring a dedicated Finance portfolio at the executive level.

cards.front: Who was the first Finance Member of the VEC (from 1859), and what tax did he introduce in 1860?
cards.back: James Wilson introduced income tax in 1860; he died in 1860 before the Act that constitutionally backed his post was passed.

cards.front: How did the Administrative Military Member and the Commander-in-Chief (CIC) differ in role within the VEC under the Indian Councils Act, 1861?
cards.back: Military Member (ordinary): ran paperwork, logistics, defence budget. CIC (extraordinary): supreme field command over the army — two hats deliberately kept separate.

cards.front: What was the composition of the VEC after a 6th Ordinary Member was added in 1874, and what portfolio did the new member hold?
cards.back: GG + 6 Ordinary Members (Home, Revenue, Finance, Law, Military, Public Works) + CIC (extraordinary member).

cards.front: How many additional members could the Viceroy nominate to the ILC under the Indian Councils Act, 1861, and what fraction had to be non-officials?
cards.back: 6 to 12 additional members, of whom at least half had to be non-officials — the first time non-officers could sit in the legislature.

cards.front: Which three Indians were first nominated to the ILC in 1862, and what did they have in common?
cards.back: Raja of Banaras, Maharaja of Patiala, and Dinkar Rao of Gwalior — all elites who had remained loyal during the 1857 revolt.

cards.front: What legislative powers did the ILC NOT have under the Indian Councils Act, 1861?
cards.back: Could not ask questions, pass resolutions, discuss or vote on the Budget, or introduce bills without the Viceroy's prior approval; Viceroy held absolute veto.

cards.front: What was the Viceroy's Ordinance power under the Indian Councils Act, 1861?
cards.back: Power to make law by executive order bypassing the legislature, valid for 6 months.

cards.front: What did the Indian Councils Act, 1861 do to reverse the centralisation that had peaked in 1833 under the Charter Act?
cards.back: Restored legislative powers to Bombay and Madras, and proposed new Provincial Legislative Councils for Bengal, Punjab, and the North-Western Provinces.

cards.front: In what years were the new Provincial Legislative Councils set up for Bengal, NWP, and Punjab under the Indian Councils Act, 1861's framework?
cards.back: Bengal — 1862; NWP — 1886; Punjab — 1897.

cards.front: Which UPSC Prelims question (2002) directly tested the Indian Councils Act, 1861, and what was its correct answer?
cards.back: Q: Which Act strengthened the Viceroy's authority by substituting the portfolio system for corporate functioning? Answer: Indian Councils Act, 1861.

cards.front: What two Western philosophical traditions formed the intellectual foundation of the Moderates?
cards.back: Utilitarianism (greatest good for the greatest number) and Liberalism (individual rights, rule of law, constitutional governance).

cards.front: What did the Moderates mean by 'Constitutional Methods'?
cards.back: Using only institutions and mechanisms the State itself provided — petitions, legislature, judiciary — to redress grievances, never street agitation.

cards.front: What was the Moderates' stated long-term political vision for India under British rule?
cards.back: Self-Government like Canada or Australia — dominion status with full British citizenship, not removal of British rule.

cards.front: What phrase did Surendranath Banerjea use to describe what the Moderates actually wanted to end?
cards.back: "Un-British Rule" — the gap between Britain's own stated liberal values and its actual conduct in India.

cards.front: What did first INC President W.C. Bonnerjee declare about the INC's attitude toward Britain?
cards.back: He declared that the INC was "loyal to the British & well-wishers of the British."

cards.front: Who was the first Muslim President of the INC, and at which session did he serve?
cards.back: Badruddin Tyabji of Bombay, at the Madras session of 1887.

cards.front: What percentage of INC membership was Hindu in the period 1892–1905, and what share were Brahmins within that?
cards.back: Hindus made up 90% of members; Brahmins alone constituted roughly 40% of the Hindu membership.

cards.front: Which pre-existing political organisation did Bengal have in 1885, and how many members did it send to the first INC session?
cards.back: The Indian Association (1876); Bengal sent only about 5 members, and only after being informed at the last moment.

cards.front: Until what year did the INC officially avoid all social questions, and why?
cards.back: Until 1907 — to maintain the fragile Hindu-Muslim-Parsi coalition, since raising caste or religious reform risked splits the British could exploit.

cards.front: What was the approximate occupational composition of INC membership in 1892–1905?
cards.back: Roughly 20% landlords, 40% lawyers, and 15% traders, most from landed families.

cards.front: What was the real motive behind British textile manufacturers in Lancashire lobbying for factory regulations in India?
cards.back: Stricter rules would raise Indian production costs and reduce Indian textile competitiveness against British goods in global markets.

cards.front: What did the Factories Act 1881 (Ripon 80–84) specifically regulate?
cards.back: Applied to factories with 100+ workers; banned child labour under 7; capped children aged 7–12 at 9 hours/day; mandated fencing of hazardous machinery.

cards.front: How did the Factories Act 1891 (Lansdowne 88–94) extend the 1881 Act?
cards.back: Coverage extended to 50+ worker factories; minimum age raised 7→9, upper child-labour age raised 12→14; women capped at 11 hours/day with 1.5-hour rest.

cards.front: What was the Indian Mines Act 1901 (Curzon 99–05) notable for?
cards.back: It was the first major regulation of mining conditions, setting a minimum age for child labour in mines and improving conditions for women and children underground.

cards.front: Why did Moderate methods ultimately fail to produce results, according to the chapter?
cards.back: Their narrow demographic (90% Hindu, lawyer-landlord classes) gave them no mass base, so the British could safely ignore petitions that carried no threat of popular disruption.

cards.front: What defence of the Moderates did Gokhale offer in 1913?
cards.back: Without the Moderates' cautious approach, the British would not have allowed the formation of the INC at all.

cards.front: What was the declared goal of the very first INC session in 1885?
cards.back: Building national unity — the Congress at Bombay explicitly declared this as its first goal.

cards.front: What rule did Dadabhai Naoroji lay down for the INC in 1886, and why?
cards.back: Congress would take up only political questions, not social or class questions, so internal divisions (caste, religion, gender) would not split the national platform.

cards.front: What was the INC's 1889 Minority Clause, and what makes it historically notable?
cards.back: INC demanded proportional reserved seats for religious minorities in the ILC and PLCs — notable because it was the INC, not the Muslim League, that first formally demanded minority representation.

cards.front: How were INC sessions structured to build inter-regional bonds across India?
cards.back: Each session rotated to a different part of the country, and the President was specifically chosen from outside the host region.

cards.front: Which three thinkers are named as the key architects of the Drain Theory?
cards.back: Dadabhai Naoroji, Romesh Chandra Dutt, and MG Ranade — with Ranade called the father of Indian economics.

cards.front: What two-volume work did Romesh Chandra Dutt publish, and when?
cards.back: The Economic History of India, published in 1901 and 1903, providing a data-driven account of how British policies impoverished India.

cards.front: What is the one-sentence core argument of the Drain Theory as stated in the chapter?
cards.back: The misuse of political power over the State of the Colony for the economic benefit of the Colonial Power.

cards.front: What is the 'commercialisation of agriculture' as defined in the chapter?
cards.back: Reorienting Indian agriculture away from food crops and towards cash crops and raw materials (cotton, indigo, jute, opium) for export to British factories. (Prelims 2018)

cards.front: Which infrastructure development cut the sea distance between India and Britain by 4,500 miles, and when was it completed?
cards.back: The Suez Canal, constructed between 1859 and 1869, cut the sea route and made extracting raw materials faster and cheaper.

cards.front: What were Council Bills, and why did the chapter describe them as a drain mechanism?
cards.back: Promissory notes issued by the India Council in London: foreign importers paid forex to London (which stayed there) and used CBs in India to buy goods, funded by Indian taxpayers — so India never received foreign exchange for its exports.

cards.front: What guaranteed return did British railway investors receive on their capital, and from when did payments start?
cards.back: A guaranteed 5% annual interest in pound sterling, starting from the day of investment — including the years the railway was still under construction.

cards.front: What were 'Home Charges' in the Drain Theory framework?
cards.back: Charges India was made to pay Britain for services supposedly rendered — covering British official salaries/pensions, EIC shareholder dividends, loan interest, SoS office expenses, stores, and War Office payments.

cards.front: By 1947, what share of cultivated area was under public irrigation, and which regions were deliberately excluded from canal investment?
cards.back: Only 25% of cultivated area; Permanent Settlement areas — Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa — received little canal investment because land revenue there could not be further raised.

cards.front: What was Dadabhai Naoroji's rebuttal to the British claim that the drain was 'only 2%' of export value?
cards.back: Even a small surplus, if invested in India rather than drained, would have compounded over decades into significant GDP growth — the drain robbed India of that compounding effect year after year.

cards.front: What did Dalhousie introduce in 1853, and what was its original stated purpose according to the chapter?
cards.back: Railways, introduced primarily for faster movement of the British army — military control was the original purpose, not Indian economic development.

cards.front: What 2022 estimate is cited in the chapter for the total value of the colonial drain at 2022 prices?
cards.back: $45 trillion, calculated by Utsa Patnaik — the chapter uses this to argue any modernisation was an unintended byproduct, not done for India.

cards.front: What dual significance did the Indian Councils Act of 1892 hold for the Moderate movement?
cards.back: It was simultaneously a result of the Moderates' struggle and proof of its failure — showing the British had listened just enough to avoid real concessions.

cards.front: Why was the word 'election' deliberately omitted from the Indian Councils Act of 1892?
cards.back: The legal mechanism was defined as 'nomination on the basis of recommendation' — it was selection, not election, so the term 'election' never appeared in the Act's text.

cards.front: Under ICA 1892, which bodies could directly recommend names for the Imperial Legislative Council?
cards.back: Only the Provincial Legislative Councils and the Bengal Chamber of Commerce could directly recommend names to the ILC; municipalities fed into PLCs, not directly into the ILC.

cards.front: How did the two-tier recommendation system under ICA 1892 work for the Imperial Legislative Council?
cards.back: Municipalities and local bodies recommended names to PLCs; PLCs then recommended names to the ILC — and the final pick in both tiers remained the Viceroy's or Governor's.

cards.front: How did the size of the Imperial Legislative Council's additional members change from ICA 1861 to ICA 1892?
cards.back: ICA 1861: 6–12 additional members (non-officials only 3–6). ICA 1892: 10–16 additional members, with at least half permitted to be non-officials.

cards.front: Despite expanding non-official membership in ICA 1892, what structural guarantee ensured the official majority remained intact?
cards.back: The Viceroy's Executive Council plus the official additional members always outnumbered non-official Indians — the official majority was mathematically guaranteed by the Act's structure.

cards.front: What happened to the Viceroy's Executive Council under the Indian Councils Act of 1892?
cards.back: The VEC did not change at all under ICA 1892; its composition and portfolios remained exactly as they stood from 1874.

cards.front: What were the three conditions attached to the new right of non-official members to ask questions under ICA 1892?
cards.back: Six days' prior notice was required, no discussion of the answers was allowed, and no supplementary questions could be asked.

cards.front: What were the two genuine new rights granted to non-official members for the first time under ICA 1892?
cards.back: The right to ask questions to the executive (with restrictions) and the right to discuss the Budget — though members could neither vote on it nor amend it.

cards.front: What was the one federalism change introduced by ICA 1892 in Centre-Province relations?
cards.back: Governors no longer needed the Viceroy's approval to nominate non-officers to their Provincial Legislative Councils — the first relaxation of Viceregal control over PLC composition since 1861.

cards.front: Who were the Secretary of State and Viceroy associated with the Indian Councils Act of 1892?
cards.back: Lord Cross was Secretary of State; Lansdowne (1888–94) was Viceroy — giving the Act its alternative name, the Lord Cross Act.

cards.front: What civil services changes were made during Lansdowne's tenure, and why must they not be listed as provisions of ICA 1892?
cards.back: On Aitchison Commission (1886–88) recommendations, CCS was renamed ICS and UCS became PCS — but these were separate administrative orders, not provisions of the Indian Councils Act of 1892.

cards.front: What demand did the Moderates formally adopt at the 1906 Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress after the disappointment of ICA 1892?
cards.back: Swaraj — self-government within the British Empire on the Dominion model, as enjoyed by Australia and Canada.

cards.front: How did ICA 1892 contribute to the rise of Extremism within the Indian national movement?
cards.back: It showed that years of petitions and rational argument produced only hollow reforms — expanded councils with no real power — cracking faith in British benevolence and the 'prayers and petitions' method.

cards.front: Which four leaders are named as the founders of the Extremist phase of the Indian National Movement by 1905?
cards.back: Lala Lajpat Rai (Punjab), Bal Gangadhar Tilak (Maharashtra), Bipin Chandra Pal and Sri Aurobindo Ghosh (Bengal).

cards.front: What did Sri Aurobindo do to avoid joining the Indian Civil Service despite qualifying?
cards.back: He deliberately skipped the horse-riding test and instead joined the Baroda Princely State civil service, later serving as Vice-Principal of Baroda College.

cards.front: Who was the first to publicly demand absolute independence, and in which year and publication?
cards.back: Sri Aurobindo was first to publicly demand absolute independence in 1907, through his writings in Bande Mataram.

cards.front: Which festivals did Tilak organise in Maharashtra to mobilise the masses for the nationalist cause, and when did each start?
cards.back: The Ganapati Festival (1893) and the Shivaji Festival (1896), both used as platforms for political mobilisation through cultural identity.

cards.front: What was the stated aim of the Indian Universities Act, 1904, and why did Indians resist it?
cards.back: Curzon brought universities under direct government control, believing they produced politically aware graduates; Indians saw it as clamping down on educated dissent.

cards.front: What were the administrative boundaries of Bengal Presidency in the period 1874–1905 (before the Partition)?
cards.back: Bengal Presidency comprised Bengal, Orissa, and Bihar; Assam existed separately as a Chief Commissioner Province.

cards.front: What two provinces did the 1905 Partition of Bengal create, and what territories did each contain?
cards.back: West Bengal (WB + Bihar + Orissa) and the new East Bengal & Assam province (East Bengal + Assam).

cards.front: What was the Indian political argument against the administrative rationale for the 1905 Bengal Partition?
cards.back: If the goal were better administration, reorganisation would have followed linguistic lines; instead the split followed the Hindu-Muslim demographic fault line, revealing communal engineering.

cards.front: What was the significance of Sakharam Ganesh Deuskar's Desher Katha (1904) and why is it a UPSC Prelims 2020 point?
cards.back: Deuskar used the word 'Desh' to mean the entire Indian subcontinent (not just Bengal), building pan-Indian economic consciousness against colonial drain.

cards.front: What happened at the Calcutta Town Hall on 7 August 1905, and why was it significant?
cards.back: Moderates including SNB, K.K. Mitra, Anand Mohan Bose, and P.C. Ray passed the Boycott Resolution against British goods and institutions — the Moderates themselves crossing into confrontational politics.

cards.front: What was the Swadesh Bandhab Samiti (1905), who founded it, and what made it notable?
cards.back: A volunteer samiti founded by Ashwini Kumar Dutt in Barisal; notable for conducting Constructive Work among Muslim ryots and organising the Barisal Conference 1906.

cards.front: What three parallel educational institutions did the Extremists establish during the Swadeshi Movement?
cards.back: The Bengal National College (with Aurobindo as principal), the National Council of Education, and the Bengal Technical Institute.

cards.front: What was the immediate flashpoint at the Surat session (1907) that caused the INC split?
cards.back: A dispute over the session's presidency — between L.L. Rai (Extremist) and Rash Behari Ghosh (Moderate) — combined with Extremist insistence on re-adopting the four Calcutta resolutions; the session collapsed with shoes and chairs hurled.

cards.front: What declaration did the Allahabad Convention (Mehta Congress) make in 1908, and how long did the INC remain divided?
cards.back: It declared 'we are loyal to the Raj'; the INC remained divided until 1920 when Mahatma Gandhi united the Moderates and Extremists.

cards.front: What happened to Tilak, Aurobindo, B.C. Pal, and L.L. Rai after the Surat Split scattered the Extremist leadership?
cards.back: Tilak was deported to Mandalay, Burma (1908–14); Aurobindo retired from politics; B.C. Pal retired temporarily; L.L. Rai went abroad 1914–20, founding the Indian Home Rule League of America.

cards.front: How did the Extremists differ from the Moderates in their goals and methods?
cards.back: Moderates: petition/prayer/press, WEMC base, goal of gradual reform within Raj. Extremists: mass mobilisation via religion/culture, Swaraj goal, methods of Boycott, Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, and Passive Resistance.

cards.front: What four resolutions did the Extremists get passed at the 1906 INC Calcutta session under President Dadabhai Naoroji?
cards.back: Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott, and National Education — the core Extremist programme adopted formally by the INC for the first time.

cards.front: What was 'Passive Resistance' as used by the Extremists during the Swadeshi Movement?
cards.back: A framework combining non-cooperation with British institutions, civil disobedience (deliberate violation of unjust laws), and the threat of violent agitation if the government responded with repression.

cards.front: Who founded the Anushilan Samiti in Calcutta, and in what year?
cards.back: Pramathanath Mitra (P. Mitra) founded it in 1902 as a body for physical training and character building with an inner purpose of armed resistance.

cards.front: Who were the three founders of the Jugantar newspaper (1906)?
cards.back: Barindra Kumar Ghosh, Bhupendranath Datta, and Abinash Bhattacharya founded Jugantar, meaning 'New Era'.

cards.front: What was Mitra Mela, and what did it become?
cards.back: Mitra Mela was a secret society set up in 1899 in Nasik by the Savarkar brothers; it was renamed Abhinav Bharat (Young India) in 1904 in Pune.

cards.front: What two works did Veer Savarkar produce while in London, and why was one banned?
cards.back: Mazzini Charitra (1906), a translation of Mazzini's writings, and The Indian War of Independence 1857 (1909), which the British banned before publication for recasting 1857 as a planned national liberation war.

cards.front: Who founded the Dacca Anushilan Samiti, and in what year?
cards.back: Pulin Behari Das founded the Dacca Anushilan Samiti in 1906, with backing from P. Mitra and Bipin Chandra Pal.

cards.front: What was the Criminal Investigation Department (CID), and what commission recommended its creation?
cards.back: A professionalised network of spies and informers established by the colonial government in 1903 to track, infiltrate, and dismantle political dissent, following the Fraser Police Commission of 1902.

cards.front: What significant act did Madame Bhikaji Cama perform at Stuttgart in August 1907?
cards.back: She unfurled the first version of the Indian national flag at the International Socialist Congress in Stuttgart, Germany.

cards.front: What was India House in London, and who set it up?
cards.back: India House was a student hostel set up by the Indian Home Rule Society (founded by Shyamji Krishna Varma in 1905) that actively promoted nationalist views among Indian students.

cards.front: How did Jugantar's revolutionary method differ from the Dacca Anushilan Samiti's under Pulin Behari Das?
cards.back: Jugantar favoured immediate spectacular acts of violence and individual heroic action; the Dacca Anushilan Samiti focused on long-term military preparation, mass organisation, and a future coordinated rebellion.

cards.front: What happened at Muzzafarpur, and who were the two revolutionaries responsible?
cards.back: Prafulla Chaki and Khudiram Bose threw a bomb at Magistrate Kingsford's carriage; Kingsford was not inside, two English women were killed, Chaki shot himself to avoid capture, and Bose was sentenced to death.

cards.front: Who defended Aurobindo Ghosh in the Alipore Conspiracy Case, and why could he not be convicted?
cards.back: C.R. Das defended Aurobindo; B.C. Pal refused to testify, and without his testimony the prosecution could not secure a conviction.

cards.front: What was the sentence given to Barindra Kumar Ghosh after the Alipore Case, and where was he sent?
cards.back: Barindra Kumar Ghosh was found guilty, sentenced to death, and his sentence was later commuted to transportation for life in the Cellular Jail (Kala Pani) in the Andaman Islands.

cards.front: What was the title of Tilak's Kesari article on the Muzzafarpur bombing, and what sentence did it earn him?
cards.back: The article was titled 'Arrival of Bomb'; Tilak was charged with sedition and sentenced to six years' imprisonment, deported to Mandalay, Burma.

cards.front: Who killed Lt. Col. William Curzon-Wyllie, and in what year and city?
cards.back: Madan Lal Dhingra killed Lt. Col. William Curzon-Wyllie in London in 1909.

cards.front: Who killed District Magistrate Jackson in the 1909 Nasik Conspiracy Case, and what was Savarkar's connection?
cards.back: Anant Laxman Kanhere killed Jackson using a pistol that Savarkar had sent from London; Savarkar was sentenced to transportation for life in 1910 as a consequence.

cards.front: Who attempted to assassinate Viceroy Hardinge in Chandni Chowk during the Delhi capital procession, and what was the outcome?
cards.back: Rash Behari Bose threw a bomb from a balcony at Hardinge seated on an elephant; Hardinge was wounded but survived.

cards.front: What was the Muslim population share in British India according to Census 1881, and where were Muslims a majority?
cards.back: Roughly 20% overall, with a majority in Punjab and roughly 50% in Bengal.

cards.front: What argument did W.W. Hunter make in Indian Musalmans (1871) and what policy did it justify?
cards.back: He argued Muslim economic decline since the end of Mughal rule fed the Faraizi movement, so the British should appease Muslims — justifying the Divide and Rule approach of favouring Muslim interests against Hindu-dominated political formations.

cards.front: What two institutions did Sir Syed Ahmed Khan (1817–98) set up, and what was the purpose of each?
cards.back: Mohammadan Anglo Oriental College, 1875 (later Aligarh Muslim University) — to combine Western education with Islamic values; Mohammadan Educational Congress, 1886 — set up as a rival to the INC, to discourage Muslim participation in it.

cards.front: What did Sir Syed Ahmed Khan mean by 'qaum', and how did it shape his politics?
cards.back: Qaum means community/nation as a distinct ethno-religious group; he argued the Hindu qaum and Muslim qaum had separate interests, making the INC unfit to represent Muslims — an early form of the Two Nation Theory.

cards.front: Who led the Simla Deputation of 1906, whom did they meet, and what three demands did they make?
cards.back: Elite Muslims led by the Aga Khan met Viceroy Minto05-10; they demanded no annulment of Bengal Partition, population-proportional reservation in the ILC, PLCs, and government jobs, and Separate Electorates in future council reforms.

cards.front: What are Separate Electorates, and why did the chapter say they 'structurally promote the Two Nation Theory'?
cards.back: Only Muslims could vote in seats reserved for Muslim candidates; this told every Muslim voter their representative must be Muslim and their interests are separate from Hindu interests, institutionally deepening communal division.

cards.front: When and where was the All India Muslim League founded, and what was its immediate trigger?
cards.back: Founded in Dacca in December 1906, immediately following the Simla Deputation, to preserve Bengal Partition and secure Separate Electorates.

cards.front: Who were Morley and Minto, and what is the formal name of the reform they gave their names to?
cards.back: John Morley was the Secretary of State for India (London); Minto05-10 was the Viceroy and Governor-General in India; the reform is formally called the Indian Councils Act, 1909 (ICA1909).

cards.front: What distinction did Morley explicitly draw between Responsible Government and what ICA1909 actually introduced?
cards.back: Morley stated there was no intent of Responsible Government via ICA1909; what it introduced was Representative Government (Limited Self-Government) — elected representatives could advise, but the Executive was not accountable to the Legislature.

cards.front: What was the structure of the expanded Imperial Legislative Council (ILC) under ICA1909, and did officials or non-officials hold the majority?
cards.back: 69 members total: 8 ex-officio + 1 rotating + 27 elected + 33 nominated (28 officials + 5 non-officials); officials held the majority at 37 versus 32 non-officials.

cards.front: Who was the first Indian inducted into the Viceroy's Executive Council under ICA1909, and in what role?
cards.back: Satyendra Prasanna Sinha (S.P. Sinha), appointed as Law Member — the first Indian in the Viceroy's Executive Council.

cards.front: How did the Muslim separate electorate seats under ICA1909 exceed population-proportional representation, and what double advantage did Muslims gain?
cards.back: Muslims were about 20% of India's population but got 8 of 27 elected ILC seats (roughly 30%); they could also vote in unreserved general seats, giving them influence in both reserved and unreserved constituencies.

cards.front: How did budget and question rights under ICA1909 differ from what ICA1892 had allowed?
cards.back: ICA1909 allowed voting on individual budget items (not the whole budget) and supplementary questions (original questioner only); ICA1892 allowed budget discussion but no voting, and no supplementary questions at all.

cards.front: Why is Minto05-10 known as the 'Father of Communal Electorate', and what long-term consequence did the chapter attribute to this?
cards.back: He presided over the introduction of separate electorates for Muslims in ICA1909; the chapter attributes this as laying the direct foundation for the partition of India in 1947.

cards.front: What term does the chapter use for the nature of government produced by ICA1909, and how does it define that term?
cards.back: Benevolent Despotism — 'benevolent' because ICA1909 was more democratic than ICA1892 (more participation and elections); 'despotism' because real power remained entirely with the British Executive, answerable to nobody in India.

cards.front: What two Indians were appointed to the Secretary of State's India Council in London in August 1907, and was this a provision of ICA1909?
cards.back: K.G. Gupta and Syed Hussain Bilgrami; this was a precursor action, not a provision of ICA1909 itself, though it led to Indian presence in the London administration for the first time.

cards.front: What were the two stages of the Ghadar Movement's overall plan?
cards.back: Stage one: build the fire abroad through narrative; stage two: light it inside India through arms and soldiers.

cards.front: Which newspaper first highlighted the irony of British Indian migration policy, and from where was it published?
cards.back: Free Hindustan (1907), published from Vancouver by Tarak Nath Das.

cards.front: What did Bakunin's concept of 'propaganda of the deed' mean in the Ghadarite context?
cards.back: Specific political acts — including violence and armed mutiny — are more powerful than speeches or pamphlets in awakening the masses.

cards.front: Where did Lala Hardayal set up his Bakunin Institute, and in what year?
cards.back: Oakland, 1912.

cards.front: Where and when was the Ghadar Party founded, and what newspaper did it launch?
cards.back: San Francisco, 1913; it launched The Ghadr newspaper the same year.

cards.front: What was the name of the patriotic poem series published in The Ghadr newspaper?
cards.back: Ghadr Di Goonj.

cards.front: Whose banned book did The Ghadr newspaper publish in serialised parts?
cards.back: Veer Savarkar's Indian War of Independence (1909).

cards.front: What were the key dates of the Komagata Maru incident, from departure to its violent end in India?
cards.back: April 1914 departed Hong Kong; May 1914 arrived Vancouver (standoff); July 1914 forced out; September 1914 arrived Budge Budge, Calcutta — Budge Budge Riot followed.

cards.front: Who led the Ghadar side of the Punjab sepoy-mutiny plot, and when was the mutiny scheduled?
cards.back: Rash Behari Bose operated in Lahore; the mutiny was scheduled for February 21, 1915.

cards.front: What was the SS Maverick operation, and what was its outcome?
cards.back: Germany financed shipping 30,000 rifles from the US to India via the SS Maverick; the ships including Annie Larsen were intercepted by US and British authorities and the arms never reached India.

cards.front: What was the Christmas Day 1915 plot, and why did it collapse?
cards.back: Revolutionaries planned a massive Calcutta uprising expecting a German arms delivery to Bengal; British intelligence cracked communication codes and intercepted the network, ending the plot before it materialised.

cards.front: Who was Bagha Jatin, and where and how did he die?
cards.back: Jatindranath Mukherjee, mastermind of the Bengal leg of the Hindu-German Conspiracy; mortally wounded at the Battle of Chasakhand/Balasore on the Burhabalanga river, Odisha, September 1915, dying in hospital the next day.

cards.front: Which four companions fought alongside Bagha Jatin at Chasakhand?
cards.back: Chittapriya Ray Chaudhuri, Manoranjan Sengupta, Niren Dasgupta, and Jyotish Pal.

cards.front: What was the Hindu-German Conspiracy (Zimmermann Plan)?
cards.back: A WWI strategy by the German Foreign Office to destabilise British India by funding and arming Indian revolutionaries, executed through three interconnected plots spanning San Francisco, Berlin, Bengal, and Punjab.

cards.front: What was the Rodda & Co. Arms Heist, and why did the Mauser C96 matter to the revolutionaries?
cards.back: Calcutta, August 1914 — Ghadarites stole Mauser C96 pistols; the hollow wooden holster converted each pistol into a short-barrelled carbine, giving five men unprecedented rapid-fire range against police.

cards.front: Why did the Ghadar sepoy-mutiny plan find little traction in the Punjab army?
cards.back: The Peel Commission post-1857 had deliberately reduced political consciousness in the army; low western education meant Ghadarite appeals found little resonance among sepoys.

cards.front: How did Udasi Sikh Mahants undermine the Ghadar Movement?
cards.back: As pro-British socially influential Gurudwara priests, they actively instructed religious masses not to support the Ghadarites.

cards.front: How did Tilak's and Besant's Home Rule Leagues differ in founder, area, HQ, and scale?
cards.back: Tilak: Bombay Province/Maharashtra (excl. Bombay city), Berar, Karnataka, Central Provinces; HQ Poona; 6 branches. Besant: Rest of British India; HQ Madras; 200 branches.

cards.front: Which city was explicitly excluded from Tilak's Indian Home Rule League's area of operation?
cards.back: Bombay city was excluded from Tilak's league's territory.

cards.front: How many branches did Besant's All India Home Rule League establish, and where was its headquarters?
cards.back: Besant's league had 200 branches, headquartered at Madras.

cards.front: What did Tilak define as the goal of Swaraj in his Home Rule League strategy?
cards.back: Self-rule within the British Empire — not the overthrow of British rule.

cards.front: What unexpected political consequence followed the British arrest of Annie Besant in 1917?
cards.back: Even Moderates joined the Home Rule Leagues, uniting INC factions against British overreach.

cards.front: What symbolic act of protest did Sir S. Subramania Iyer perform after Besant's arrest in 1917?
cards.back: He renounced his knighthood (K.C.I.E.) and wrote an explosive letter to US President Woodrow Wilson.

cards.front: How do G. Subramania Iyer and Sir S. Subramania Iyer differ in their key roles?
cards.back: G. Subramania Iyer: journalist, co-founded The Hindu (1878), moved the first INC resolution in 1885. Sir S. Subramania Iyer: judge, knighthood surrendered, co-founder and Honorary President of the Home Rule League Madras (1916).

cards.front: Why was the English newspaper The Hindu founded in 1878?
cards.back: To protest the appointment of an Anglo-Indian judge over a native Indian candidate.

cards.front: Who moved the first resolution at the very first session of the INC in Bombay in 1885?
cards.back: G. Subramania Iyer moved the historically significant first resolution.

cards.front: What did 'Passive Resistance' mean to the Extremists during the Home Rule League era, as drawn from Aurobindo Ghosh's 1907 doctrine?
cards.back: First, a comprehensive boycott of British goods, schools, courts, and administrative roles (non-cooperation); then, if the State responded with coercive laws, the duty to deliberately break those laws and accept punishment (civil disobedience).

cards.front: What did the Lucknow Pact (1916) demand regarding the composition of the Viceroy's Executive Council?
cards.back: At least 50% Indians in the Viceroy's Executive Council.

cards.front: What did the Lucknow Pact (1916) agree to retain regarding Muslim representation, and what did it demand about council membership?
cards.back: It agreed to continue Separate Electorates and demanded an expanded council with an elected majority and direct elections as broad as possible.

cards.front: On what terms did the Lucknow Pact (1916) seek self-government, and how did this compare to a full Dominion Status demand?
cards.back: Self-government at an early date, equal to other Self-Governing Dominions — less than immediate full self-rule; the exact phrase 'Dominion Status' appeared only in the Motilal Nehru Report of 1928.

cards.front: Which 1911 British policy reversal was seen by the Muslim League as a massive betrayal, contributing to the Lucknow Pact's Congress-League rapprochement?
cards.back: The annulment of the Bengal Partition (1905), which had created a Muslim-majority east Bengal that the Muslim League had supported.

cards.front: What was Tilak's famous statement on untouchability, and at which conference did he deliver it?
cards.back: "If God tolerates untouchability then I won't recognise him as God" — delivered at the 1918 All India Depressed Classes Conference.

cards.front: What did the Montagu Statement of 20 August 1917 declare as British policy for India?
cards.back: Gradual development of self-governing institutions with a view to the progressive realisation of responsible government in India within the British Empire.

cards.front: What is the Montagu-Chelmsford Report (1918), and what did it directly produce?
cards.back: A joint report by Secretary of State Montagu and Viceroy Chelmsford16-21 after Montagu's personal tour of India; it directly led to the Government of India Act, 1919.

cards.front: What kind of central legislature did the Government of India Act, 1919 introduce for the first time?
cards.back: A bicameral legislature: the Central Legislative Assembly (lower house, ~145 members) and the Council of States (upper house, ~60 members).

cards.front: What was the term (life) of the Central Legislative Assembly and the Council of States under the Government of India Act, 1919?
cards.back: Central Legislative Assembly: 3 years; Council of States: 5 years.

cards.front: How did the Government of India Act, 1919 change Muslim separate electorates compared to the Indian Councils Act, 1909?
cards.back: Under the Indian Councils Act, 1909, Muslims could vote in both Muslim reserved seats and unreserved seats; under the Government of India Act, 1919, Muslims could no longer vote in unreserved seats — the electorates became watertight.

cards.front: Which communities received separate electorates for the first time under the Government of India Act, 1919, beyond Muslims?
cards.back: Sikhs, Anglo-Indians, and Christians — all with watertight electoral rolls, voting only in their own reserved constituencies.

cards.front: How did the Government of India Act, 1919 handle women's right to vote?
cards.back: It did not directly grant women the vote; it empowered Provincial Legislative Assemblies to pass resolutions removing the sex disqualification, subject to the same strict property qualifications as men.

cards.front: What did Section 96C of the Government of India Act, 1919 mandate, and what came of it?
cards.back: It mandated a Public Service Commission for India; the Commission was established in 1926 with Ross Barker as its first Chairman — the direct institutional ancestor of the modern UPSC.

cards.front: What reform did the Government of India Act, 1919 introduce for the Indian Civil Service examination?
cards.back: It mandated the ICS examination be held simultaneously in India alongside England; the first examination in India was held in 1922.

cards.front: What was the Narendra Mandal, and how was it brought into existence?
cards.back: A Chamber of Princes created as a purely advisory body for Princely States; recommended by the Montagu-Chelmsford Report and formally constituted by Royal Proclamation in 1921, not by the Government of India Act, 1919 itself.

cards.front: What powers did the Viceroy retain over the central legislature under the Government of India Act, 1919?
cards.back: Veto over all bills, power to approve bills rejected by the legislature, ordinance power (valid 6 months), power to restore cuts in grants, and 75% of budget items were non-votable.

cards.front: What does 'Dyarchy' mean, and at which level of government did it apply under the Government of India Act, 1919?
cards.back: Dual rule (Dy = Two; Archy = Top Authority); it applied at the provincial level, splitting subjects into Reserved and Transferred categories governed by different authorities.

cards.front: Under Dyarchy, how did Reserved subjects differ from Transferred subjects in terms of authority and accountability?
cards.back: Reserved (Law & Order, Police, Finance, Land Revenue, Irrigation, Control over Officials): governed by the Governor, no accountability to the PLA. Transferred (health, education, local government, agriculture): governed by Ministers responsible to the PLA.

cards.front: Why was Irrigation kept as a Reserved subject under Dyarchy rather than transferred to Indian ministers?
cards.back: To protect British investor returns: canals across the Indus, Ganga, and Krishna-Godavari belts were built through FDI by British investors, and keeping Irrigation under the Governor shielded those returns from elected Indian ministers.

cards.front: What structural flaw made it impossible for Indian ministers to govern even their Transferred subjects effectively under Dyarchy?
cards.back: Indian ministers had no control over finance or the bureaucracy — without money and without control over officials, they could not deliver on health, education, or agriculture even when these were nominally their subjects.

cards.front: What incident at Pietermaritzburg railway station in 1893 became Gandhi's political catalyst?
cards.back: Gandhi was ejected from a first-class compartment solely for being Indian, despite holding a valid ticket.

cards.front: How long did Gandhi ultimately stay in South Africa, and why did he extend his visit?
cards.back: Twenty-two years — the Indian community, leaderless and without an educated advocate, persuaded him to stay and fight for them.

cards.front: What choice did the Immigration Law Amendment Bill force on indentured labourers who finished their contracts?
cards.back: Leave South Africa, re-indenture for two more years, or pay an annual poll tax of £3.

cards.front: What two institutions did Gandhi found during the Constitutional Phase (1896–1906) to give Indians an organised voice?
cards.back: The Natal Indian Congress and the newspaper Indian Opinion.

cards.front: What five personal qualities did Gandhi require of a true Satyagrahi?
cards.back: Truthfulness, non-violence, fearlessness, readiness to accept suffering, and love toward the wrongdoer.

cards.front: What book inspired Gandhi to establish the Phoenix Settlement in 1904, and where was it located?
cards.back: John Ruskin's Unto This Last; the settlement was established near Durban and also printed Indian Opinion.

cards.front: Why was the Asiatic Law Amendment Act 1906 called the 'Black Act'?
cards.back: It required every Indian to carry a Registration Certificate at all times; failure to produce it meant fine, imprisonment, or deportation.

cards.front: What did Gandhi do first when the government offered to withdraw the Black Act if Indians voluntarily registered?
cards.back: Gandhi was the first to register, leading by example — but the government then broke its promise and did not withdraw the Act.

cards.front: What was Tolstoy Farm, and why did Gandhi establish it in 1910?
cards.back: A communal settlement near Johannesburg, named after Leo Tolstoy, set up as a residential base for Satyagrahis and their families during the struggle.

cards.front: What two specific demands did Gokhale advise Gandhi to focus the movement on after his 1912 visit?
cards.back: Abolition of the Poll Tax under the Immigration Law and abolition of the Registration Certificate requirement under the Black Act.

cards.front: What 1913 South African Supreme Court ruling suddenly widened the mass base of Gandhi's movement?
cards.back: The court declared only Christian marriages legally valid — Hindu, Muslim, and other rites were unrecognised, making Indian wives legally not wives and children potentially illegitimate.

cards.front: Whose arrest galvanised the Indian worker community during the 1913 final struggle?
cards.back: Kasturba Gandhi's arrest — it prompted all Indian workers across the province to go on strike.

cards.front: What unprecedented diplomatic pressure came from within the British Empire during the 1913 campaign?
cards.back: Viceroy Hardinge publicly condemned the South African government's treatment of Indians.

cards.front: What were the three concrete concessions the South African government granted Gandhi at the end of the struggle?
cards.back: Poll Tax abolished; Registration Certificate requirement dropped; Hindu, Muslim, and other rite marriages given legal recognition.

cards.front: In which month and year did Gandhi return to India after his South Africa years, and how?
cards.back: January 1915 — returning not as a defeated petitioner but as a leader who had won all three key demands.

cards.front: What is the most authentic source of Gandhi's ideology, and how was it written?
cards.back: Hind Swaraj (1909), written during a ten-day sea voyage as a dialogue between a 'Reader' and an 'Editor.'

cards.front: What does 'Cultural Nationalism' mean, and how did Gandhi extend this tradition beyond his predecessors?
cards.back: Cultural Nationalism roots national identity in civilisation and heritage; Gandhi uniquely converted it into a concrete economic and political programme, dressing like the masses and using shared civilisational symbols such as Ram Rajya to mobilise across class and caste.

cards.front: What did Gandhi mean by 'Enlightened Anarchism'?
cards.back: True self-rule achieved when individuals attain perfect moral self-regulation, eliminating any need for a coercive State or even representative democracy.

cards.front: How did Gandhi's vision of Swaraj differ from the Home Rule of the Extremists and the class rule of Marx?
cards.back: Gandhi's Swaraj meant every individual being his own master through moral self-regulation — not national Home Rule, not indirect democracy, and not class-based rule.

cards.front: What model of governance did Gandhi prefer over Western parliamentary democracy, and which constitutional provision reflects it?
cards.back: Village Republics based on direct democracy and mutual cooperation; Article 243 of the Constitution, establishing the Gram Sabha under Panchayati Raj, is his most concrete institutional legacy.

cards.front: What was Gandhi's concept of Trusteeship?
cards.back: A capitalist holds his enterprise as a trustee — ownership stays, but its purpose shifts to the welfare of workers and the broader community, not personal profit alone.

cards.front: What method did Gandhi prefer for resolving disputes between workers and capitalists, and what did it involve?
cards.back: Arbitration — transparent inquiry into the capitalist's balance sheet and the worker's cost of living to find a just middle path, avoiding strikes or lockouts.

cards.front: Why did Gandhi's demand for universal disarmament have a specific Indian colonial context?
cards.back: The Arms Act of 1878 under Viceroy Lytton76-80 disarmed Indian civilians while exempting Anglo-Indians and Eurasians, making disarmament a colonial tool; Gandhi demanded it be universal to end this asymmetry.

cards.front: What is Satyagraha, and what are its five components as stated in the chapter?
