cards.back: Literally 'truth-force' or 'soul-force' — an extra-constitutional, non-violent mass struggle comprising Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Constructive Work, Non-Violence, and Spirituality/Morality.

cards.front: What was Gandhi's first standing principle regarding the conduct of a Satyagrahi toward an opponent?
cards.back: Do not benefit from the weakness of the evil doer — a Satyagrahi takes only what has been earned through moral force, not through the opponent's vulnerability.

cards.front: What does the S-CW-S rhythm of Gandhi's mass movements stand for, and why was the middle phase never idle?
cards.back: Struggle–Constructive Work–Struggle; the Constructive Work phase built atmashakti, trained Satyagrahis, strengthened the INC network, and raised grassroots awareness to prevent economic desperation from turning violent.

cards.front: Why did Gandhi deliberately never define Swaraj precisely as a political goal?
cards.back: To maximise the movement's support base across India's social plurality — Swaraj meant end of high rents to a peasant, better wages to a worker, dignity to a woman, and self-governance to a nationalist intellectual.

cards.front: What triggered Gandhi's 1932 'Epic Fast' and what was its outcome?
cards.back: Ramsay MacDonald's Communal Award granted separate electorates to Depressed Classes; the fast led to the Poona Pact — Ambedkar accepted joint electorates with reserved seats rising from 71 to 147.

cards.front: How did Gandhi's 1947 Calcutta fast differ in trigger and outcome from his 1948 Delhi fast?
cards.back: Calcutta (September 1947): spiralling Hindu-Muslim riots post-Partition — the 'Calcutta Miracle' stopped violence within days. Delhi (January 1948): attacks on Muslims by Hindu and Sikh refugees — leaders signed a seven-point pledge; Gandhi was assassinated twelve days after breaking the fast.

cards.front: Which of Gandhi's publications was launched specifically to campaign against untouchability, and when?
cards.back: Harijan (English), Harijan Bandhu (Gujarati), and Harijan Sevak (Hindi) — all launched in 1933 after Young India ceased, with the anti-untouchability campaign as their central focus.

cards.front: At which trial in India did Gandhi formally appear in a courtroom, plead guilty, and ask for the maximum penalty?
cards.back: The Great Trial of 1922 before Judge C.N. Broomfield at the Ahmedabad Sessions Court, arising from three seditious articles in Young India; Gandhi was sentenced to 6 years and held at Yerwada Central Jail.

cards.front: Who brought Gandhi to Champaran, and at which INC session did they meet?
cards.back: Rajkumar Shukla, a peasant leader from Bihar, met Gandhi at the Lucknow Session of the INC in 1916.

cards.front: What was the Tinkathia System that drove the Champaran Satyagraha?
cards.back: A contract forcing ryots to cultivate indigo on 3/20th (three kathas out of every twenty) of their land for British planters.

cards.front: What act of Civil Disobedience did Gandhi perform when British authorities ordered him to leave Champaran?
cards.back: He refused to comply with the official order to leave the district and courted arrest — the defining act of Civil Disobedience.

cards.front: Which legislation abolished the Tinkathia System, and in what year was it passed?
cards.back: The Champaran Agricultural Act, 1918, though planter oppression did not fully stop even after its passage.

cards.front: What was the workers' original demand in the 1918 Ahmedabad mill strike, and what wage increase did arbitration finally award?
cards.back: Workers demanded a 50% wage increase; the Arbitration Board settled on 27.5%.

cards.front: What labour organisation did the Ahmedabad mill strike of 1918 directly lead to founding?
cards.back: The Textile Labour Association, formed in 1920.

cards.front: Why was the Kheda Satyagraha of 1918 classified as Non-Cooperation rather than Civil Disobedience?
cards.back: Ryots withheld land revenue because the law entitled them to remission on crop failure — they disputed the government's violation of its own law, not colonial sovereignty itself.

cards.front: Which future national leader became a follower of Gandhi through the Kheda Satyagraha?
cards.back: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel — Kheda was his first experience of organised mass action.

cards.front: What was the formal name of the Rowlatt Act passed in February 1919, and which committee recommended it?
cards.back: The Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act, based on recommendations of a sedition committee chaired by Justice S.A.T. Rowlatt.

cards.front: Why was the Rowlatt Act considered a broken promise by Gandhi?
cards.back: It extended wartime emergency powers of the Defence of India Act 1915 into peacetime, at the very moment the Montague Statement (1917) had spoken of India's gradual march toward self-government.

cards.front: What were the two historic firsts achieved by the Rowlatt Satyagraha of April 1919?
cards.back: It was the first mass strike and the first all-India movement in Indian history.

cards.front: What was the official British death toll from the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, and what did the INC count?
cards.back: British official records counted 379 dead; the INC's count was 1,500 dead.

cards.front: Which treaty triggered the Khilafat Movement among Indian Muslims, and what were their core demands?
cards.back: The Harsh Treaty of Sèvres (1920) — demands were to revise it, restore the Khalifa's dignity and suitable territory, and ensure Arabs were not placed under non-Muslim rule.

cards.front: Who set up the Khilafat Committee in March 1919, and who were they?
cards.back: Muhammad Ali Jauhar and Shaukat Ali — the Ali Brothers — set up the Khilafat Committee in March 1919.

cards.front: Who presided over the Special Calcutta Session of September 1920, and what three goals did it adopt for the NCM?
cards.back: Lala Lajpat Rai presided; the three goals were Swaraj, redressal of Punjab wrongs, and redressal of Khilafat wrongs.

cards.front: What were the two key structural reforms to the INC passed at the Nagpur Session of December 1920?
cards.back: A Congress Working Committee of 15 members as top executive body, and Provincial Congress Committees reorganised on linguistic lines.

cards.front: What happened at Chauri Chaura in 1922, and how did Gandhi respond?
cards.back: Police fired on satyagrahis killing 3; the crowd retaliated burning 22 policemen alive — Gandhi withdrew the NCM and suspended the planned CDM at Bardoli.

cards.front: Why did the Khilafat Movement end in 1924?
cards.back: The people of Turkey abolished the Khalifate and established a secular republic under Mustafa Kemal Ataturk — an external decision that dissolved the movement's entire basis.

cards.front: Who founded the UP Kisan Sabha in February 1918, and what role did each founder play?
cards.back: Gauri Shankar Mishra and Indra Narayan Dwivedi were operational organisers; Madan Mohan Malaviya served as senior political patron lending his weight.

cards.front: Why was Jawaharlal Nehru NOT associated with the UP Kisan Sabha of 1918?
cards.back: Nehru engaged the Kisan Sabha movement only from June 1920 onwards, when he visited Pratapgarh with Baba Ramchandra.

cards.front: What were abwabs and nazrana in the context of Awadh peasant grievances?
cards.back: Extra cesses imposed by landlords on tenants beyond the legal rent, with no authorisation.

cards.front: Why did Baba Ramchandra set up the Awadh Kisan Sabha in 1920, separate from the existing Kisan Sabha?
cards.back: Malaviya, a Moderate, refused to support Non-Cooperation, so Ramchandra (with Nehru's support) formed the Awadh Kisan Sabha for extra-constitutional struggle.

cards.front: How did the British end the Awadh Kisan Sabha agitation of 1921?
cards.back: Through repression under the Seditious Meetings Act (1911) and a legislative concession — the Awadh Rent Amendment Act (1921) — which addressed rent grievances.

cards.front: Who led the Eka Movement of 1921 in Awadh, and what made this leadership significant?
cards.back: Madari Pasi, a leader from the lower castes — showing the peasant struggle drew leaders from the most oppressed sections of rural society, not just upper castes.

cards.front: How did the Eka Movement differ from Gandhian peasant movements, and what was the consequence?
cards.back: Eka did not adhere to non-violence, unlike Gandhian movements; this gave the British easy grounds to repress it as a law-and-order matter, and it was crushed by 1922.

cards.front: Who were the Jenmies in the context of the Mapilla Revolt (1921)?
cards.back: Predominantly Hindu hereditary landowners in Malabar who controlled vast tracts of land and subjected Mapilla Muslim tenants to heavy rents and arbitrary eviction.

cards.front: Why did the Mapilla Revolt (1921) turn communal, and how did the British respond?
cards.back: When INC leaders were arrested, the movement lost organised guidance; agrarian anger against Jenmie landlords shifted into Hindu-Muslim violence, and the British declared martial law.

cards.front: What was the specific grievance behind the Borsad Satyagraha (1922–24) that made it unique?
cards.back: The government imposed an additional tax on villagers to fund extra police, while that police force was itself in monetary collusion with the dacoits it was meant to stop.

cards.front: What outcome ended the Borsad Satyagraha, and who ordered it?
cards.back: The Governor of Bombay, upset over the police-dacoit collusion accusation, ordered an inquiry — leading to an immediate halt to confiscations and withdrawal of the additional tax.

cards.front: What was the original government assessment increase that triggered the Bardoli Satyagraha (1928), and what did the tribunal eventually revise it to?
cards.back: Government imposed a 30% increase in land revenue; the independent tribunal revised it down to 6.03%.

cards.front: What title did Vallabhbhai Patel receive at Bardoli, and from whom?
cards.back: "Sardar" — conferred by the women and ryots of Bardoli.

cards.front: What was the Hali system that Gandhi opposed in Bardoli before the 1928 satyagraha?
cards.back: A system of hereditary forced labour and alcohol addiction that trapped low-caste Kaliparaj peasants in a debt cycle, binding them to landlords across generations.

cards.front: What triggered the Akali Movement's foundation, specifically regarding the Golden Temple Mahants?
cards.back: The Mahants honoured General Dyer after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919, triggering widespread Sikh outrage and protests against Mahant control of Gurudwaras.

cards.front: What were the SGPC and SAD formed for respectively within the Akali Movement?
cards.back: SGPC (1920) for organised management of the Golden Temple; SAD for further organised protests to wrest control of other Gurudwaras beyond the Golden Temple from Mahants.

cards.front: Why did the British ultimately pass the Gurudwara Reform Act, 1925, conceding Akali demands?
cards.back: The British feared disaffection in the Army, since Sikhs formed a significant part of the British Indian Army — they conceded out of military necessity, not on principle.

cards.front: Into what three factions did the Akalis split after the movement, and which political group did each become?
cards.back: Gandhians and Leftists → Kirti Kisan Party; Communalists → continued as Akali Dal; Loyalists to the British → formed the Unionist Party.

cards.front: Who were the five founders of the Hindustan Republican Army (HRA) in 1924?
cards.back: Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqullah Khan, Jogesh Chatterjee, Chandrashekhar Azad, and Sachin Sanyal.

cards.front: What was the stated goal of the HRA (1924)?
cards.back: Armed revolution to establish a 'United States of India' with universal adult franchise.

cards.front: What book did Sachin Sanyal write, and what was it about?
cards.back: Bandi Jeevan — a guide to revolutionary activities; he was also associated with the Delhi Conspiracy Case of 1912.

cards.front: What was the Kakori Robbery Case (1925), and what were its consequences for HRA leaders?
cards.back: HRA members looted cash from a train to buy arms; Ram Prasad Bismil and Ashfaqullah Khan were hanged, while Chandrashekhar Azad escaped.

cards.front: What did the addition of 'Socialist' in the name HSRA (1928) signify compared to HRA (1924)?
cards.back: It reflected the leftward ideological shift of revolutionaries — now committed to ending both colonial and class oppression, influenced by the Russian Revolution of 1917.

cards.front: How did Bhagwati Charan Vohra die, and when?
cards.back: Killed on 28 May 1930 while testing a bomb near the River Ravi, Lahore — a significant loss to HSRA.

cards.front: Who was the intended target of Bhagat Singh's assassination attempt in the Lahore Conspiracy Case, and who was actually killed?
cards.back: Target was James Scott (SP who ordered the lathi-charge on Lala Lajpat Rai); John Saunders (DSP) was killed instead in a case of mistaken identity.

cards.front: How and where did Chandrashekhar Azad die on 27 February 1931?
cards.back: He shot himself at Alfred Park (now Chandrashekhar Azad Park), Allahabad, rather than surrender to the British.

cards.front: Why did Bhagat Singh and B.K. Dutt throw a bomb in the Central Legislative Assembly in 1929?
cards.back: To protest the Public Safety Bill and Trade Disputes Bill targeting the working-class movement; the bomb was harmless — intended to 'make the deaf hear,' not to kill.

cards.front: What phrase did the leaflets carry when Bhagat Singh and B.K. Dutt threw the bomb in the CLA?
cards.back: 'To make the deaf hear' — the intention was to draw attention to the anti-labour bills, not to harm anyone.

cards.front: Who led the Chittagong Armory Raid (1930) and what organisation did he set up?
cards.back: Surya Sen, a school teacher, set up the Indian Republican Army (IRA) and led the raid while Gandhiji's CDM was underway.

cards.front: Why was the Chittagong Armory Raid (1930) historically significant in the context of armed struggle?
cards.back: It was the first instance of group action in armed struggle since 1857; it also mobilised women and Muslims as fighters.

cards.front: Who were Shanti Ghosh and Suniti Chaudhary, and what did they do on 14 December 1931?
cards.back: School girls aged 15 and 14 respectively; they shot dead C.G.B. Stevens, the District Magistrate of Comilla.

cards.front: What did Pritilata Waddedar do to avoid capture by the British?
cards.back: Aged 21, she consumed potassium cyanide and became a martyr during the Chittagong revolutionary struggle.

cards.front: What essay did Bhagat Singh write in jail in 1930, and what did it argue?
cards.back: 'Why I Am an Atheist' — it rejected religious dogma and affirmed his commitment to reason and revolutionary ideals.

cards.front: What happened to Jatin Das during the hunger strike in jail, and on which day did he die?
cards.back: Fellow prisoner of Bhagat Singh, Jatin Das died on the 64th day of the hunger strike due to forced feeding, protesting inhuman prison conditions.

cards.front: Why was the Simon Commission appointed 2 years ahead of the GOI Act 1919's 10-year review schedule?
cards.back: The Conservative Government did not want to leave this politically sensitive matter to the next government; pressure from Pro Changers, rising revolutionary activity, and fear of communism spreading in India also drove early appointment.

cards.front: Which future British Prime Minister sat on the seven-member Simon Commission?
cards.back: Clement Attlee, who became Prime Minister of Britain (1945–51) and oversaw Indian independence.

cards.front: On what precise ground did INC oppose the Simon Commission?
cards.back: Not a single Indian was included among its 7 members, violating the principle of self-government promised in the Montague Statement of 1917.

cards.front: Who challenged Indians to draft a constitution themselves, and what was his prediction about their ability to do so?
cards.back: Secretary of State for India Birkinhead challenged Indians, believing their internal differences would prevent them from acting unitedly on a draft constitution.

cards.front: What triggered the lathi charge on Lala Lajpat Rai in Lahore, and what was the outcome?
cards.back: Anti-Simon Commission protests during the Commission's second visit to India in October 1928; SP James Scott ordered the charge, and Lajpat Rai died from his injuries in November 1928.

cards.front: What was the Nehru Report (August 1928), and why is it historically significant?
cards.back: A constitutional blueprint drafted by a committee under Motilal Nehru within the All Party Conference — the first Indian attempt at drafting the principles of a constitution.

cards.front: What form of self-government did the Nehru Report demand, and what powers would Britain retain under it?
cards.back: Dominion Status — sovereignty would remain with the British Crown, which would retain power over Defence, Foreign Policy, and the right to change the constitution; Indians would have self-government in domestic affairs.

cards.front: What structural arrangement did the Nehru Report propose for the relationship between British India and the Princely States?
cards.back: A Union of India bringing both together with federal relations between them, while British India itself would have a unitary structure with residuary powers at the Centre.

cards.front: Which franchise provision did the Nehru Report demand for the first time clearly in Indian constitutional history?
cards.back: Universal Adult Franchise — the first time it was explicitly and clearly demanded in an Indian constitutional proposal.

cards.front: What was the Nehru Report's position on separate electorates for Muslims?
cards.back: Separate electorates were rejected outright — a major blow to ML1906.

cards.front: On what condition did the Nehru Report agree to separate Sindh from the Bombay Presidency?
cards.back: Only after Dominion Status was achieved and only if Sindh was financially viable — a conditional concession, not the unconditional separation ML1906 had demanded.

cards.front: What compromise did INC reach at the Calcutta session (December 1928) on the question of Purna Swaraj vs Dominion Status?
cards.back: INC approved the Nehru Report but resolved that if Dominion Status was not granted within one year, its goal would become Purna Swaraj and it would launch a Civil Disobedience Movement.

cards.front: What were Jinnah's 14 Points (March 1929), and what was their long-term significance?
cards.back: A summary of every communal demand ever made by any Muslim organisation, issued after failure of the Four Delhi Proposals and Three Calcutta Amendments; it became the blueprint for all future political actions of ML1906.

cards.front: What was the key finding of the Butler Committee Report (1929) regarding the Princely States and a future Union of India?
cards.back: British Paramountcy over Princely States was re-affirmed, and Princely States should not be transferred into a Union of India without their own consent.

cards.front: What did Viceroy Irwin's Diwali Declaration (31 October 1929) actually offer to Indians regarding Dominion Status?
cards.back: It stated only an intent — no decision, no timeline, and a Round Table Conference in London (not a Constituent Assembly in India) as the mechanism; nothing concrete was offered.

cards.front: Why did INC respond to the Diwali Declaration with the Delhi Manifesto in November 1929?
cards.back: Because the Diwali Declaration offered no concrete commitment — only a vague future intent and a London-based Round Table Conference rather than a Constituent Assembly in India.

cards.front: Who was INC President at the Lahore Session of December 1929, and what was the key demand rejected by Irwin that led to it?
cards.back: Jawaharlal Nehru presided; Viceroy Irwin had rejected the Delhi Manifesto, which sought dominion status via an RTC acting as a Constituent Assembly.

cards.front: Why did MG issue 11-point demands in January 1930 instead of launching CDM immediately?
cards.back: To offer the British a chance to deliver the substance of Swaraj without confrontation — if they complied, INC would sacrifice its own claim to political power.

cards.front: What exchange-rate demand featured in MG's 11-point list, and why did Indian capitalists want it?
cards.back: A rupee rate of 1s 4d (down from 1s 6d fixed in 1926 by the Hilton-Young Commission), to make Indian exports cheaper and reverse the advantage British goods had in India.

cards.front: From where did MG begin the Dandi March, and when was the Sabarmati Ashram founded?
cards.back: MG marched from the Sabarmati Ashram (founded 1917) to the Dandi coast to break the salt law in March 1930.

cards.front: Why did C. Rajagopalachari choose 13 April 1930 as the launch date for the Vedaranniyam March?
cards.back: It coincided with both the Tamil New Year (Puthandu) and the anniversary of the Jallianwala Bagh massacre — two powerful emotional triggers in one day.

cards.front: Who was the first woman in India to pay a penalty for violation of the salt laws?
cards.back: Rukmini Lakshmipathi, during the Vedaranniyam March led by C. Rajagopalachari.

cards.front: Which district in Odisha was called the 'Second Dandi', and which two women leaders were prominent there?
cards.back: Inchudi in Balasore district, notable for massive women's participation under Rama Devi and Malati Choudhury.

cards.front: Which Karnataka town earned the title 'Bardoli of Karnataka' during CDM, and what was its main campaign?
cards.back: Ankola in Uttara Kannada, known for intense no-tax and salt campaigns including raids on the Sanikatta salt works.

cards.front: What were the Khudai Khidmatgars, who founded them, and by what popular name were they known?
cards.back: A volunteer brigade ('Servants of God') founded in 1929 by Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, popularly called the Red Shirts or Surkh Posh; their uniforms were dyed with cheap brick-dust.

cards.front: What happened when British-commanded Royal Garhwal Rifles were ordered to fire on the crowds at Qissa Khwani Bazaar in April 1930?
cards.back: Led by Chandra Singh Garhwali, the soldiers refused to shoot unarmed civilians; they were court-martialled and given severe prison sentences for mutiny.

cards.front: Who led the Dharsana raid after Abbas Tyabji and Kasturbai Gandhi were arrested before reaching the salt works?
cards.back: Sarojini Naidu, MG's son Manilal, and Imam Saheb took charge on 21 May 1930; about 2,500 volunteers faced 400 police armed with steel-tipped lathis.

cards.front: Which journalist's eyewitness report of the Dharsana raid turned international opinion against British rule, and where was it published?
cards.back: Webb Miller of United Press; his report was published in over a thousand newspapers worldwide.

cards.front: What was the British government's primary reason for agreeing to the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of March 1931?
cards.back: The 1st RTC of 1930 had failed without INC, proving that no constitutional settlement would carry popular legitimacy without INC's participation.

cards.front: Why did the 2nd Round Table Conference (September–December 1931) fail?
cards.back: A deadlock over separate electorates: all minorities including the Depressed Classes (represented by Ambedkar) demanded them, while MG and INC opposed them.

cards.front: What was the outcome of the 3rd Round Table Conference (November–December 1932)?
cards.back: Held without INC (banned since January 1932), it produced a White Paper (1933) examined by a Joint Parliamentary Committee, whose report became the basis of the Government of India Act 1935.

cards.front: What was the Communal Award of August 1932, and what was INC's official stance on it?
cards.back: Announced by British PM Ramsay MacDonald, it extended separate electorates to the Depressed Classes; INC neither accepted nor rejected it, as the demand came from the Depressed Classes themselves.

cards.front: Who signed the Poona Pact of September 1932 on behalf of the Lower Castes and the Upper Castes respectively?
cards.back: B.R. Ambedkar signed for the Lower Castes; Madan Mohan Malviya signed for the Upper Castes.

cards.front: What was MG's objection to the Communal Award, and what did the Poona Pact substitute in its place?
cards.back: MG opposed separate electorates (not greater reservation); the Pact replaced them with reserved seats in joint electorates, more than doubling the number of reserved seats.

cards.front: Who was the third woman to preside over the INC, at which session, and what distinguished her from her predecessors?
cards.back: Nellie Sengupta (born Edith Ellen Gray in Cambridge) presided at the 1933 Calcutta Session — the second foreign-born woman president, after Annie Besant (1917) and Sarojini Naidu (1925).

cards.front: What did the Simon Commission (1927) recommend regarding dyarchy at the provincial level?
cards.back: Abolition of dyarchy introduced under GOI 1919 and replacement with full responsible government in the provinces, though with some emergency powers retained by the Governor.

cards.front: Which Round Table Conference did the INC participate in, and what were its demands that went unfulfilled?
cards.back: The 2nd RTC (1931); INC demanded a federation with responsible government at the Centre and Purna Swaraj — both rejected, and the Nehru Report of August 1928 remained unfulfilled.

cards.front: Why did the federal provisions of the Government of India Act 1935 never come into operation at the Centre?
cards.back: At least 50% of Princes had to sign the Instrument of Accession as defined in Section 6 of GOI 1935 — that threshold was never met.

cards.front: Which subjects did a Princely State transfer to the Union Government upon signing the Instrument of Accession under GOI 1935?
cards.back: Only Defence, Foreign Affairs, and Communications were transferred to the Union Government.

cards.front: What were the four Reserved Subjects under the proposed central dyarchy in GOI 1935?
cards.back: Defence, External Affairs, Ecclesiastical Affairs (Church), and Tribal Areas — under absolute Legislative and Executive control of the Viceroy.

cards.front: What did Nehru describe as 'the only major change' in the entire Government of India Act 1935?
cards.back: Financial control over British India was transferred from the Secretary of State for India in London to the Viceroy in India.

cards.front: What was the Federal Court established under GOI 1935, and when was it actually set up?
cards.back: The first court with jurisdiction over disputes between provinces and between provinces and the Centre; it was actually set up in 1937.

cards.front: How did elections to the Federal Assembly differ from those to the Council of States under GOI 1935, and why?
cards.back: FA elections were indirect (to limit INC strength in the more powerful lower house); CoS elections were direct for better regional and community representation.

cards.front: What share of the central Budget under GOI 1935 was non-votable, and what power did the Viceroy retain over it?
cards.back: 80% of the central Budget was non-votable; the Viceroy retained residual powers, veto powers, ordinance powers, power to restore cuts, and power to certify rejected bills.

cards.front: Under GOI 1935, what innovation did Scheduled Castes receive in electoral representation compared to GOI 1919?
cards.back: For the first time, Scheduled Castes received reservation in elected seats (FA, CoS, and PLAs) under joint electorates — up from only nominated seats under GOI 1919.

cards.front: What was the constitutional innovation in GOI 1935 regarding distribution of legislative subjects, and what did it later become?
cards.back: GOI 1935 introduced for the first time a proper federal distribution into three lists — Federal, Concurrent, and Provincial — the ancestor of the 7th Schedule of the Constitution of India 1950.

cards.front: From what year did the provincial provisions of the Government of India Act 1935 actually come into force?
cards.back: 1937 — and the end of dyarchy meant all provincial subjects became transferred subjects under PLAs and popular ministers.

cards.front: What share of the provincial Budget under GOI 1935 was non-votable, and which Governor power most directly foreshadowed Article 356 of the Constitution of India 1950?
cards.back: 40% of the provincial Budget was non-votable; the Governor's power to take over the government and run it indefinitely directly foreshadowed Article 356.

cards.front: How did a Separate Electorate differ from a Reserved Seat in British Indian constitutional law?
cards.back: Separate Electorate strictly segregated the voter pool by identity (only community members vote for their candidate); a Reserved Seat guaranteed a candidate from a group but the voter pool could be broader.

cards.front: How did the Muslim electoral arrangement change from the Indian Councils Act 1909 to the Government of India Act 1919?
cards.back: 1909: Muslims had a 'Double Vote' — they could vote in both Muslim and General constituencies. 1919: strict segregation; cross-voting banned and watertight separate rolls created.

cards.front: Under which Act were direct elections first introduced for the Central Legislative Assembly and Council of States?
cards.back: The Government of India Act 1919 introduced direct elections for the first time for the CLA, CoS, and PLAs.

cards.front: Why did the INC decide to form governments under the provincial provisions of GOI 1935 after the 1937 elections?
cards.back: To prevent non-INC parties from occupying the space (the same logic as the Pro-Changers entering the CLA in 1923), and to promote Constructive Work — now with executive as well as legislative power.

cards.front: What was one lasting effect of the 28-month Congress Ministries (1937–39) on the Princely States?
cards.back: INC's rise to power in provinces inspired people in the Princely States; new Praja Mandals and State People's Congresses were set up and existing SPCs saw rising membership.

cards.front: What did '@ToP' stand for as a study tag in Ch 43's four-question framework?
cards.back: Transfer of Executive Power at the Centre — meaning a powerless Viceroy, an Indian Prime Minister, and Indian ministers accountable to an elected legislature.

cards.front: Why did the majority of INC leaders privately favour an Allied victory in WW II, despite British arrogance in declaring India a belligerent?
cards.back: They feared an Axis victory could hand India to Japan and eliminate all progress made by the Indian National Movement.

cards.front: What three demands did the INC place before Britain in 1939 in exchange for supporting the war effort?
cards.back: Immediate responsible government at the Centre; a Constituent Assembly after the war; and a declaration of British war aims regarding India's future freedom.

cards.front: At which Congress session did Bose defeat Gandhi's preferred candidate Pattabhi Sitaramayya for the presidential election?
cards.back: The Tripuri Session (1939), prompting Gandhi to declare 'Pattabhi's defeat is my defeat.'

cards.front: What organisation did Subhas Chandra Bose form after resigning from the INC presidency in 1939, and what was its stated aim?
cards.back: The Forward Bloc (1939) — a left-wing faction aimed at consolidating the left wing within Congress so as to capture the INC from within.

cards.front: Who coined the word 'Pakistan', and where — and what is notable about the 1940 Lahore Resolution's use of that word?
cards.back: Choudhary Rahmat Ali coined it in his 1933 pamphlet 'Now or Never'; the 1940 Lahore Resolution itself never used the word 'Pakistan' — the press and public attached the name to it later.

cards.front: What were the five key provisions of the August Offer (AO1940) made by Viceroy Linlithgow36-43?
cards.back: Advisory War Council; expanded VEC with more Indians; Constituent Assembly after the war (mainly Indians); Dominion Status after the war; no future constitution without minority consent.

cards.front: What was historically significant about AO1940's promise on constitution-making, compared to all previous British offers?
cards.back: It was the first time Britain formally promised that framing the constitution would be 'primarily the responsibility of Indians themselves.'

cards.front: Why did the Muslim League (ML1906) reject the August Offer despite the veto clause in its favour?
cards.back: The Offer made no explicit mention of Pakistan or two separate Constituent Assemblies, leaving ML with no guarantee that a Hindu-majority government would not simply ignore the veto and prevent Pakistan's creation.

cards.front: Who were the first three Individual Satyagrahis (in order) and under which law were they arrested?
cards.back: Vinobha Bhave, Nehru, and Brahma Dutt — arrested in that order under the Defence of India Act, 1939.

cards.front: What was the specific, narrow demand of Individual Satyagraha launched in October 1940 — and what was it deliberately NOT about?
cards.back: Freedom of speech (protesting the Defence of India Act, 1939) — it was deliberately not a demand for Purna Swaraj.

cards.front: How did the 1941 expansion of the Viceroy's Executive Council change Indian representation, and what key portfolios were still excluded?
cards.back: Indians rose from 3 of 8 to 8 of 12 members — a first majority — but Defence, Home, and Finance portfolios remained outside their reach.

cards.front: What strategic events in 1941–42 compelled Britain to send the Cripps Mission to India?
cards.back: Germany attacked the USSR (June 1941), Japan attacked Pearl Harbour (December 1941), and Japan occupied Rangoon/Burma (March 1942), exposing India's eastern border.

cards.front: Who led the Cripps Mission, and who were the INC's official negotiators with it?
cards.back: Sir Stafford Cripps (minister in Churchill's War Cabinet) led it; Nehru and Maulana Azad (the serving INC President) were the INC's official negotiators.

cards.front: How did the Cripps Mission's proposed Constituent Assembly differ from the August Offer's version on the question of membership?
cards.back: AO1940 promised a Constituent Assembly of 'mainly' Indians (some British possible); Cripps upgraded this to solely Indian members for the first time.

cards.front: What was the most explosive provision of the Cripps Mission, and how many separate entities could it theoretically produce?
cards.back: Any Province or Princely State disagreeing with the framed constitution could secede — potentially 565 Princely States + 11 Provinces = 576 separate entities.

cards.front: On which single point did the Cripps talks actually break down?
cards.back: Defence — the British refused to transfer Defence portfolio to Indian ministers during the war, retaining the Viceroy's full powers over it.

cards.front: What phrase did Gandhi use to describe the Cripps offer, and what did it mean?
cards.back: A 'post-dated cheque' — most benefits were deferred until after the war, and nothing was of immediate effect.

cards.front: Who coined the phrase 'Quit India', and what other famous slogan is he credited with?
cards.back: Yusuf Meherally coined both 'Quit India' and 'Simon Go Back'.

cards.front: Why did the Communist Party of India (CPI) not join the Quit India Movement?
cards.back: The Soviet Union was fighting on the British side in World War II, and the CPI followed that political line.

cards.front: What made the Quit India Movement the first truly all-India mass movement?
cards.back: It was the first mass movement to include the Princely States alongside British India.

cards.front: Which mission's failure in 1942 directly triggered the decision to launch the Quit India Movement?
cards.back: The failure of the Cripps Mission in 1942, which offered only vague post-war promises with no real transfer of power.

cards.front: Where and on what date did the INC formally pass the Quit India Resolution?
cards.back: At a special INC session in Bombay on 8th August 1942, followed by a public meeting at Gowalia Tank (Azad Maidan).

cards.front: What was Gandhi's 'Do or Die' call, and in which language was its slogan?
cards.back: 'Karo ya Maro' — Gandhi's call to the public at Gowalia Tank on 8th August 1942 laying out the plan of action.

cards.front: What was the first recorded parallel government during the Quit India Movement, who led it, and where?
cards.back: Ballia, eastern UP (August 1942), led by Chittu Pandey, who overthrew the District Collector and freed INC leaders from jail.

cards.front: How did the Jatiya Sarkar of Midnapore differ from the Patri Sarkar of Satara in duration and activities?
cards.back: Jatiya Sarkar (December 1942 – September 1944): arbitration courts, rice distribution, cyclone relief, Vidyut Vahini armed wing; Patri Sarkar (mid-1943 – 1945): people's courts, village libraries, prohibition, Gandhi Marriages with Dalit inclusion — the longest-running and most successful.

cards.front: Who set up the Patri Sarkar of Satara, and which leader earned the title 'Lion of Satara'?
cards.back: Nana Patil set it up; Achyut Patwardhan provided guidance and earned the title Lion of Satara.

cards.front: What role did Usha Mehta play during the underground phase of the Quit India Movement?
cards.back: Usha Mehta ran the Congress Radio to coordinate underground activities.

cards.front: How many people had been arrested in British repression of the Quit India Movement by the end of 1942?
cards.back: 60,000 people had been arrested by the end of 1942.

cards.front: What was the first time the INC explicitly raised a no-rent campaign as part of its programme?
cards.back: During the Quit India Movement (1942), when the private plan instructed tenants to pay only fair rent and only to anti-British zamindars.

cards.front: Where was Gandhi held during his 21-day fast, and what did the British demand he do before the fast?
cards.back: Gandhi was held at Aga Khan Palace, Pune; the British wanted him to condemn the movement's violence — he refused and fasted instead.

cards.front: Who was Mahadev Desai, when did he die, and where?
cards.back: Gandhi's personal secretary, who died on 15 August 1942 in Aga Khan Palace — Gandhi described his loss as losing his right hand.

cards.front: Which region saw the highest mass participation in the Quit India Movement, and why?
cards.back: Eastern UP and Bihar, where the INC had done the highest level of constructive work, translating directly into organised participation.

cards.front: In what sense was the Quit India Movement both 'spontaneous' and 'not spontaneous'?
cards.back: Spontaneous at the top — arrests on 9 August left the public without the full plan; not rootless below — decades of INC grassroots work and the 1940–41 Individual Satyagraha had prepared ordinary people to act.

cards.front: What event in June 1945 formally marked the end of the Quit India Movement?
cards.back: All INC leaders were released in June 1945 to participate in the Simla Conference, formally ending the movement.

cards.front: What did the resignation of Indian members of the Viceroy's Executive Council during Gandhi's fast reveal?
cards.back: That the British administrative machinery was breaking from within — its own Indian members refused to be held responsible for Gandhi's possible death.

cards.front: What was the primary cause of the Bengal Famine of 1943 according to the chapter?
cards.back: It was a man-made famine, not a crop failure — caused by food diversion, loss of Burma imports, poor distribution, and war-driven speculation.

cards.front: Approximately how many Indians died in the Bengal Famine of 1943?
cards.back: Roughly 5 million Indians died.

cards.front: What did Viceroy Linlithgow propose regarding Bengal's food crisis, and how did Churchill respond?
cards.back: Linlithgow requested food for India and proposed a ban on food exports from Bengal; Churchill denied both requests.

cards.front: What did the Famine Inquiry Commission (1945) conclude, and who headed it?
cards.back: Headed by Sir John Woodhead, it largely blamed natural factors and supply disruption, and was criticised for not holding the colonial administration adequately accountable.

cards.front: What is Amartya Sen's 'entitlement failure' theory as applied to the Bengal Famine?
cards.back: Famines occur not from absolute food shortage but from populations losing access to food — via collapsed wages, speculation-driven prices, and procurement policies draining rural markets.

cards.front: Who conceived the INA and from which pool of men was its First Division formed in September 1942?
cards.back: Captain Mohan Singh conceived it by organising Indian PoWs; 40,000 PoWs from Singapore joined the First Division.

cards.front: Why was Captain Mohan Singh arrested by the Japanese in December 1942?
cards.back: He had demanded a primary role and genuine autonomy for the INA in any attack on British India, creating friction with Japanese command.

cards.front: What was the Indian Independence League (IIL), when and where was it founded, and how did it relate to the INA?
cards.back: Set up in Bangkok, Thailand in June 1942 by Pritam Singh, Swami Satyananda Puri, and others; the IIL was the political organisation and the INA was its military arm.

cards.front: Under what disguise and route did Subhas Chandra Bose escape from house arrest in Calcutta in January 1941 to reach Germany?
cards.back: He escaped disguised as an Afghan, travelled through Afghanistan into the USSR, then continued disguised as 'Orlando Mazzotta' through Italy, arriving in Germany in March 1941.

cards.front: What assurance did Netaji extract from Japanese General Tojo before launching the INA campaign?
cards.back: That Japan did not want to annex India after victory — ensuring the INA's fight was for Indian independence, not a Japanese empire.

cards.front: On what date did Netaji establish the Provisional Government of Free India, and where was its headquarters?
cards.back: 21st October 1943, with headquarters in Rangoon (Burma) and Singapore.

cards.front: What names did Netaji give to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands when he visited them in December 1943?
cards.back: The Andamans were renamed 'Shaheed Dweep' and the Nicobars 'Swaraj Dweep'; he hoisted the flag at Gymkhana Ground on 29–31 December 1943.

cards.front: What was the Rani Jhansi Regiment and what was significant about it?
cards.back: An all-women NRI regiment raised by Netaji, symbolically named after the most iconic figure of the 1857 revolt.

cards.front: Who were the three accused in the most famous INA trial held at the Red Fort in November 1945?
cards.back: Shah Nawaz Khan, Prem Sehgal, and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon.

cards.front: What did the British themselves admit about the INA agitations in terms of their scale within the Indian National Movement?
cards.back: The British stated that no issue in the entire history of the Indian National Movement had generated so much sympathy among Indians.

cards.front: Which INC lawyer fought cases for the accused INA men at the Red Fort trial?
cards.back: Bullabhai Desai, lawyer and INC leader in the Central Legislative Assembly.

cards.front: What were the three grievances of the naval ratings whose strike triggered the Naval Ratings Mutiny in February 1946?
cards.back: Fear of post-war unemployment, poor service conditions and racial discrimination in salaries, and inspiration from the INA agitations.

cards.front: Which ship did the Naval Ratings Mutiny begin on, and what flags did the ratings hoist?
cards.back: It began on HMIS Talwar; ratings hoisted tricolour flags alongside flags of the INA, the INC, and the Muslim League.

cards.front: Who advised the naval ratings during the mutiny despite opposition from Gandhi and the INC?
cards.back: Aruna Asaf Ali advised the ratings and provided leadership.

cards.front: What 'martial races' myth did the Naval Ratings Mutiny shatter, and why was that myth strategically significant to British rule?
cards.back: The myth that certain Indian communities were inherently loyal to the Crown and would always enforce imperial authority against other Indians — the entire edifice of British India rested on using Indian soldiers against Indians.

cards.front: How many main planks did the Rajaji (C.R.) Formula of 1944 contain?
cards.back: Three main planks — though the chapter does not enumerate them individually beyond this count.

cards.front: What did the Gandhi–Jinnah talks on the Rajaji Formula reveal about Jinnah's strategy?
cards.back: The talks showed Jinnah exactly how far INC was willing to bend; he found the answer useful as a minimum base for future negotiations.

cards.front: What was the outcome of the Gandhi–Jinnah talks held on the Rajaji Formula?
cards.back: The talks failed completely — Jinnah's demands were very different from what Rajagopalachari had proposed.

cards.front: Who negotiated the Desai-Liaqat Pact of 1945, and in which body did they serve?
cards.back: Bullabhai Desai (INC) and Liaqat Ali Khan (ML1906) — both leaders in the Central Legislative Assembly.

cards.front: What share of seats did the Desai-Liaqat Pact propose for INC and ML1906 in the Viceroy's Executive Council?
cards.back: 50% of Indian minister seats to INC and 50% to ML1906; the Governor General and Commander-in-Chief remained non-Indian.

cards.front: Why did the Desai-Liaqat Pact fail?
cards.back: Jinnah refused to acknowledge any knowledge of the pact — using it to establish a minimum floor, knowing each INC concession raised his next demand.

cards.front: At which conference was the Wavell Plan of 1945 discussed, and what event immediately preceded it?
cards.back: The Shimla Conference in June 1945, held after INC leaders imprisoned during the Quit India Movement (1942–45) were released.

cards.front: On what single point did the Wavell Plan collapse?
cards.back: ML1906 insisted Muslim ministers in the VEC come only from ML1906 — not from INC's own Muslim leaders — and Wavell refused to guarantee this.

cards.front: What political consequence did the failure of the Wavell Plan have for ML1906?
cards.back: Wavell's announcement amounted to an implicit veto for ML1906 on transfer of power, enormously boosting ML1906's prestige and helping it win the December 1945 elections in Muslim-reserved seats.

cards.front: Who were the three members of the Cabinet Mission that arrived in India in February 1946?
cards.back: Lord Pethick-Lawrence (Secretary of State for India), Sir Stafford Cripps (President of the Board of Trade), and A.V. Alexander (First Lord of the Admiralty).

cards.front: What did 'compulsory grouping' mean in the Cabinet Mission Plan 1946, and why did it matter?
cards.back: Muslim-majority provinces were required to join their prescribed group (B or C), making CMP1946 a One-State, Two-Nation solution — and giving Jinnah implicit partition within a united India.

cards.front: Who served as Provisional President when the Constituent Assembly first convened on 9 December 1946, and who was elected permanent President two days later?
cards.back: Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha was Provisional President; Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent President on 11 December 1946.

cards.front: According to historian Bipin Chandra, on what two counts did INC fail, leading to partition?
cards.back: INC failed to bring Muslims into the national movement as a mass constituency, and failed to curb Muslim communal forces — especially from 1937 onwards.

cards.front: What effect did each INC concession — Lucknow Pact, Rajaji Formula, Desai-Liaqat Pact — have on ML1906's negotiating position?
cards.back: Each concession raised ML1906's floor for the next negotiation, increasing its prestige rather than building goodwill or reducing its demands.

cards.front: Which organisation did Lala Lajpat Rai lead as the first all-India organisation of workers in Indian history, and in what year was it founded?
cards.back: All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC), founded in 1920; it represented India at the ILO of the League of Nations from the outset.

cards.front: Who founded the Madras Labour Union (1918), and what was its significance?
cards.back: B.P. Wadia founded it; it was the first modern organised trade union in India.

cards.front: What was the CPI's fatal strategic error following the 6th World Congress of the Comintern (1928)?
cards.back: CPI declared the INC a party of the bourgeoisie and opposed the Civil Disobedience Movement, severing itself from India's largest mass movement.

cards.front: Who was the first to celebrate May Day in India (1923), and in which city?
cards.back: M. Singaravelu Chettiar celebrated it in Madras; he also presided over the Kanpur CPI conference of 1925.

cards.front: What was the Girni Kamgar Union (GKU), and which leader built it into a formidable force?
cards.back: A militant trade union built by S.A. Dange during the six-month Bombay Textile Strikes of 1928, becoming one of India's most powerful unions.

cards.front: What did the Trade Union Act of 1926 grant for the first time, and what was the irony surrounding it?
cards.back: It gave trade unions legal recognition, protected union funds, and granted strike immunity — enacted by the same colonial government that simultaneously used the Meerut Case to suppress labour.

cards.front: What did CR Das argue at the Gaya Session of 1922 that finally shifted the INC's position on workers and peasants?
cards.back: If Congress ignored workers and peasants, they would launch independent class movements that would fragment the national coalition, so their demands must enter the nationalist programme.

cards.front: What was FICCI's declared position on negotiating with the British on economic issues?
cards.back: FICCI refused to negotiate with the British government on constitutional or economic issues without the approval or participation of the INC.

cards.front: What was the Bombay Plan (1944), who drafted it, and what did it propose?
cards.back: First-ever national economic plan for India, drafted by eight industrialists including JRD Tata and GD Birla, proposing a mixed economy with heavy state investment to double per capita income in 15 years.

cards.front: Why did Indian capitalists and Moderate INC leaders oppose the Factory Acts of 1881 and 1891?
cards.back: The Acts were pushed by the Lancashire lobby to raise Indian production costs; Moderates saw them as weakening infant Indian industries already under pressure from British competition.

cards.front: What was the Poona Pact (September 1932), and why did Ambedkar describe signing it as one of the worst days of his life?
cards.back: Dalits retained reserved seats but with joint electorates instead of separate ones, surrendering the key instrument of electoral independence Gandhi's fast had forced Ambedkar to concede.

cards.front: What did Ambedkar do at the Mahad Satyagraha (1927), and what symbolic act followed at the same conference?
cards.back: He led 15,000 Dalits to draw water from a public tank, then publicly burnt the Manusmriti in December 1927 at the same Mahad conference.

cards.front: What were the core differences between Gandhi's and Ambedkar's approaches to ending caste oppression?
cards.back: Gandhi sought moral reform within Hinduism through upper-caste penance; Ambedkar demanded statutory safeguards, reservation, and if needed, exit from Hinduism altogether.

cards.front: Who was the first woman elected President of the INC, and in what year?
cards.back: Sarojini Naidu was elected INC President in 1925, the first woman to hold that position.

cards.front: What did the All India Women's Conference (AIWC, 1927) do differently from the INC regarding women's issues?
cards.back: Unlike the INC, AIWC directly took up women's education, political rights, marriage reform, and workers' rights — placing the INM first but addressing women's own demands.

cards.front: What were the core demands of the AIKS Kisan Manifesto of August 1936?
cards.back: Abolish zamindari, tax agricultural wealth on a graduated scale, cancel hereditary peasant debts, and grant tenants occupancy rights to prevent arbitrary eviction.

cards.front: What was the Tebhaga Movement (1946–47) and what intellectual groundwork had already been laid for its central demand?
cards.back: Bengal sharecroppers demanded two-thirds of produce instead of half; the Floud Commission (1940) had already recommended restructuring the landlord-tenant share but the Bengal government never implemented it.

cards.front: How did the AIKS grow despite the INC's Haripura resolution (1938), and what happened to its leadership by the early 1940s?
cards.back: AIKS reached over 800,000 members by 1939; the CPI took practical organisational control, causing both Sahajanand Saraswati and NG Ranga to eventually leave.
